  "circle describes strong college preparation and alumni success while square describes poor instructional effectiveness": "Circle claims objective preparatory outcomes: “I entered college far ahead of my peers… SHG not only prepared my for college, but for life,” whereas Square asserts instruction is inadequate: “the teaching is below average… I myself find it impossible to learn in that atmosphere.”",
  "square reports outdated instructional materials and restrictive textbook policies while circle does not": "Square documents resource decay and a restrictive policy: “outdated books that date as far back as the 1970's… They are not allowed to take the books home with them which affect their classroom performance,” a specific materials problem not mentioned in Circle.",
  "square reports widespread classroom disorder and safety concerns while circle reports a calm, supportive learning environment": "Square gives concrete examples of misbehavior and unsafe climate: “students talking, running around the classroom, play fighting… doing each other s hair… I myself find it impossible to learn,” while Circle repeatedly describes a positive environment: “we love the environment SHG has created for us.   "circle reports small class sizes or explicitly low student counts while square reports teacher vacancies and unstaffed classes": "Circle includes class size evidence from a teacher: “from a teacher with her 9 students,” indicating small classes, while Square reports staffing gaps: “some of my classes don't even have teachers (english).”",
  "square reports administrative restructuring that removed supervisory oversight and caused staff exits while circle portrays respected leadership": "Square names a damaging policy change and staff loss: “When a bogus superintendent eliminated all supervisory positions, things got worse… The best people are always forced out,” whereas Circle says leadership is highly regarded: “The leadership at the school from the principal to coaches is so revered by the student body.”",
  "circle emphasizes a faith based community and explicit school mission while square does not": "Circle invokes an institutional faith identity and motto as an operational part of the school: “SHG is a fantastic school with the motto: 'academic excellence in a community of faith',” a defining programmatic characteristic absent from Square.",
  "circle highlights well maintained facilities while square highlights decayed or insufficient resources": "Circle directly praises infrastructure: “Excellent facilities,” whereas Square points to failing resources like decades‑old textbooks: “outdated books that date as far back as the 1970's,” indicating divergent facility/resource conditions.",
  "square reports active staff turnover and loss of strong personnel affecting school quality while circle credits long term staff impact on student success": "Square links leadership decisions to loss of talent: “The best people are always forced out,” implying turnover harming quality, while Circle credits sustained staff impact: “As a Sacred Heart‑Griffin Illumni, I can say first‑hand that my SHG education was second to none… I credit a significant portion of my success to SHG.”",

}"]

  "circle reports better facilities cleanliness and stricter on-campus security than square": "Circle reviewers note campus condition and safety: “The school campuses are great,” “Also, the security at the schools is very strict and makes me feel at ease,” and “the school is clean and has good lunch food.” Square reviews praise academics and staff but do not highlight facilities or strict security measures.",

  "square reports pandemic-related health management failures and COVID-era operational problems; circle does not mention pandemic issues": "Square explicitly describes COVID management problems: “they had to shut down because too many people got sick… told me I was being too worried about covid… They fail to work with people with medical problems during this pandemic.” Circle contains no references to pandemic operations or health-management incidents.",
  "square reports institutional resource shortfalls and consequences (state funding loss and an on-site student daycare) whereas circle reports none of these institutional constraints": "Square documents broader institutional impacts: “People in this school have lost funding and representation as a school from the State of Maine and have to have a student daycare center for student parents.” Circle offers no accounts of state funding loss, reduced representation, or on-campus daycare facilities.",

  "circle highlights a high-performing, standout band program while square does not report comparable exceptional arts programming": "Circle singles out the band as “one of the best in the state” and praises directors who “went above and beyond,” whereas Square contains no mention of an outstanding music or arts program.",

["{
  "square reports a divisive mascot controversy and racist staff behavior while circle does not": "Square explicitly documents a racially offensive team name and mascot and staff condoning racism: “It’s absolutely horrendous in the year 2018 to have a racial slur as a team name, and a charicature for a mascot” and a coach who says “we need to get over slavery,” whereas Circle contains no mention of any mascot controversy or racially charged staff behavior.",

  "square offers more formal advanced and vocational programs and credentials than circle": "Square lists concrete programs and credentials: \"He takes AP classes\" and \"The Pathways available (ranging from Ag, Cosmetology,Information Technology, etc) are phenomenal giving our kids certifications upon graduation,\" whereas Circle mentions no AP, pathways, or certification programs.",
  "circle reports greater access to outdoor and recreational facilities than square": "Circle claims \"students' access to the outdoors and recreation is unrivaled,\" a facility/amenity claim that does not appear anywhere in Square's descriptions of that school.",
  "square reports administrative unresponsiveness and organizational problems that circle does not": "Square contains explicit complaints about administration and operations such as \"It's like trying to speak to the President when trying to contact them,\" \"This School is VERY unorganized,\" and \"Bad administration, doesn’t value students education,\" while Circle describes staff and faculty as \"very personable\" with no administrative complaints.",
  "square reports staff misconduct in athletics while circle reports no such misconduct": "Square accuses athletic staff of dishonesty: \"The athletic coached LIE to the Parents and students in order to get them To participate,\" whereas Circle makes no mention of coach misconduct or similar staff malfeasance.",
  "square documents active organized sports participation while circle highlights general outdoor/recreation access instead": "Square notes student involvement in teams: \"participates in sports,\" whereas Circle refers broadly to \"access to the outdoors and recreation\" without indicating organized athletic programs or team participation.",
  "square describes leadership and enrollment changes affecting school capacity while circle does not": "Square explicitly links improvements to structural changes: \"opening of Centennial High School. It cut the student population in half\" and notes a \"'new' Principal seems to have made a difference,\" whereas Circle gives no account of recent enrollment shifts or leadership turnover.",
  "circle emphasizes individualized developmental improvement while square emphasizes credentialed outcomes and course-taking": "Circle foregrounds personalized growth: \"their strengthens honored, and their weaknesses improved,\" focusing on individual development, while Square emphasizes formal academic and career outcomes: \"He takes AP classes\" and Pathways that \"giv[e] our kids certifications upon graduation.\""
}"]

  "circle reports bullying and sexual harassment incidents and ineffective responses from staff whereas square does not": "Circle details personal and systemic safety concerns: \"I've been bullied quite a bit...\" and cites \"sexual orientation and sexual harassment\" with the school \"rarely will address the issue unless contacted by a parent,\" while Square makes no mention of bullying, harassment, or poor incident response.",
  "circle reports gaps in medical and special-needs support (no first-aid staff, poor health management) whereas square does not": "Circle states concrete health-staff failures: \"There is NO first aide person on staff\" and \"Teachers and faculty do not work well with children that have a disabilities or any kind of health management routine,\" a problem absent from Square's endorsement.",
  "circle documents a competency-based assessment system that increases student stress and contributes to depression/anxiety whereas square claims effective real-world preparation": "Circle warns about the grading system: \"Our new system is the 'competency system'... the stress this can put on its students is enormous\" and links it to \"legitimate problems with depression and anxiety,\" while Square asserts the school \"gave me tons of opportunities and prepared me for the real world.\"",
  "circle reports poor teacher and counselor responsiveness and communication whereas square does not": "Circle includes multiple complaints about staff communication: \"A lot of teachers will not respond to emails or return phone calls\" and \"counsellors and staff do nothing to help you,\" whereas Square suggests positive outcomes without noting any communication or counseling failures.",
  "circle describes inconsistent routines and lack of structure for younger students whereas square does not": "Circle criticizes early-education practices: \"There is no routine or structure in this school which is very detrimental to a preschooler learning routine\" and \"They do not have regular recess hours,\" while Square offers no statements about schedules, routines, or preschool preparedness.",
  "circle reports active district public-relations efforts and local families opting out of attendance whereas square does not": "Circle claims the district uses PR to attract nonresident students because locals are leaving: \"the district has a fabulous public relations team... because the kids who live in Fraser are choosing to NOT attend and go to a better school elsewhere,\" a community-enrollment dynamic absent from Square.",
  "circle contains mixed and contradictory evaluations (both strong praise and detailed criticisms) whereas square contains only an unqualified positive endorsement": "Circle alternates between praise (\"Amazing Staff, amazing students and a great facility,\" \"I graduated well prepared for college\") and serious criticisms (administration, safety, health support), while Square only states positive outcomes: \"Great school... I am glad my child went here.\""

["{
  "square reports more drugs, violence, and alcohol problems than circle": "Square explicitly states systemic safety and substance problems: \"The school has a serious problem with : drugs, violance, academics, and admestration\" and \"Violence, drugs, and alcohol are all problems in our city.\" Circle contains no comparable claim about pervasive substance use or physical safety incidents.",
  "square reports greater staff favoritism and unprofessional misconduct toward students than circle": "Square accuses staff of selective caring and misconduct: \"The staff doesn't care unless you're a favorite of theirs\" and \"Most teachers will flirt with female student,\" whereas circle contains multiple statements that \"The teachers here really do care\" and no allegations of flirting or similar misconduct.",
  "square reports explicit program-based neglect and elitism (only certain programs matter) while circle does not": "Square claims funding and attention are funneled into select programs: \"If you're not in either program, you don't matter\" referring to sports and New Tech; circle does not describe program-based exclusion or students being ignored because they are outside flagship programs.",
  "square reports visible poor campus maintenance and cleanliness more than circle": "Square complains about physical upkeep: \"Bird droppings and trash are all over the place,\" a concrete facilities problem that circle's reviews do not mention.",
  "square reports a prioritization of athletics spending over academics more than circle": "Square criticizes resource allocation: \"Our school decided to spend 5 MILLION on a SPORTS facility, when our education department is lacking severely. Sports are what is focused on most,\" while circle does not describe a comparable large-scale athletic funding decision dominating academic resources.",
  "circle reports an explicit religious identity and curriculum emphasis on religion more than square": "Circle repeatedly identifies as a Catholic school and curricular focus on religion: \"The focus was on religion, academics, and sports\" and \"I have always been in a Catholic school,\" whereas square contains no mention of religious identity or religion-focused curriculum.",
  "circle reports strict uniform and dress code enforcement prioritized by staff more than square": "Circle states staff emphasize dress and uniforms: \"teachers and staff care more about dress code rather than education\" and \"You get used to the uniforms and of course the strict dress code,\" while square gives no indication of uniform or strict dress policy.",
  "circle reports greater teacher engagement and perceived support for student academic and social growth than square": "Multiple circle reviewers claim supportive staff and student progress: \"The teachers here really do care and want you to do well,\" \"my son has made great strides both academically and socially,\" whereas square contains claims that \"Many of the teachers are inadequate who don't interact well with the students\" and \"The staff doesn't care unless you're a favorite.\"",
  "circle reports documented alumni long-term academic and professional success more than square": "Circle includes a retrospective alumni outcome: \"I thrived at Ludden and went on to a successful college and professional career,\" signaling long-term positive outcomes; square contains praise for an individual student's programs but no explicit long-term professional outcome claim.",
  "circle reports limited exposure to cultural and religious diversity more than square": "A circle reviewer notes a curricular/community limitation: \"The only downsides ... was lack of exposure to multiple cultures and religions,\" a specific sociocultural limitation not mentioned in square.",
  "circle documents an administrative change linked to decline in school quality more than square": "Circle contains a direct causal claim about leadership turnover: \"After that, new administration took over, and it was all down hill from there,\" whereas square complains about administration generally (\"admestration\") but does not describe a discrete administrative change causing decline.",
  "circle reports improved student behavior and safety relative to previous urban schooling experiences more than square": "One circle reviewer contrasts past unsafe schooling with improvement at this school: \"When I went to Ludden, all that changed\" referring to cessation of daily fights and improved moral environment; square instead reports ongoing violence and disorder within the school/community."
}"]

  "square privileges advanced Cambridge students with a dedicated counselor and better teachers more than circle": "Square states explicitly that “if you are in advanced programs, such as Cambridge, you have access to an amazing education, with excellent teachers and a dedicated counselor who deals with only Cambridge students,” describing a program-specific assignment of superior staff and counseling that circle does not report.",

  "circle documents tolerated Confederate-symbology and explicit lack of racial diversity more than square": "Circle asserts the school “has no diversity and allows bullying to occur daily.   "circle highlights renovated facilities and documented AP/college-credit successes more than square": "Circle notes the school was “completely renovated with nice facilities” and that both children “graduated with over 21 college credits (AP) … and both received full scholarships,” emphasizing facility upgrades and measurable AP/college outcomes more prominently than square.",
  "square reports concrete operational and safety lapses in food service and athletic facilities more than circle": "Square contains concrete complaints such as cafeteria food problems — “I once bought a bag of chips, and it was from 2007… chips that expired 3 years ago” — and limited athletics infrastructure (“they don't even have a football field or track”), matters not raised in circle.",
  "square emphasizes administrative focus on standardized-test metrics and FCAT performance more than circle": "Square accuses leadership of fixating on testing: “The principal has no leadership skills whatsoever, he only cares about the FCAT,” and critiques overemphasis on FCAT that shapes priorities, a test-centered administrative focus not described in circle.",
  "circle reports pervasive classroom boredom and low daily academic rigor more than square": "Circle reports students are “bored every single day. There is never classwork or homework.   "circle identifies lack of formal teacher training plans by administration more than square": "Circle bluntly states “Teachers are untrained and administrators do not have a plan to train them,” calling out an absence of organized professional development plans by leadership, whereas square critiques evaluation frequency rather than the existence of training programs.",
  "square highlights gaps in teacher evaluation and calls for more frequent teacher assessments more than circle": "Square includes calls that “The teachers classes should be evaluated more often” and notes teacher disengagement (e.g., teachers ‘only care about getting into their goals’), focusing on the need for evaluation rather than the training-planning failures emphasized in circle.",
  "square describes ethnic/linguistic majority culture that marginalizes non-Hispanic students more than circle": "Square contains repeated claims that non-Hispanic students are alienated — “My daughters are not hispanic and are outcasted” and “The Hispanics here are stuck up… they even talk in their own language about you” — indicating an ethnic/linguistic majority climate that sidelines minorities, a dynamic different from circle’s residency/wealth-based exclusion themes."

  "square concentrates higher-quality teaching within selective programs more than circle": "Square describes an uneven instructional distribution: \"Oakland Tech has great academics... for about 25% of the school\" and \"The same students, who are in the 'best' academies or in Paideia usually have the best teachers\" indicating higher-quality instruction is concentrated in selective tracks; circle does not describe this pattern of concentrated teacher quality.",

  "square reports uneven funding and erratic building/district support more than circle": "Square explicitly blames ratings on \"uneven quality of funding and school district support\" and \"erratic building support\" while circle praises \"well maintained facilities\" and district professionalism.",
  "square reports greater fragmentation of student social life by academic tracks than circle": "Square: \"Oakland Tech is a divided community...   "circle reports more pervasive adult monitoring of student behavior than square": "Circle: \"The staff also was always in your business, so you really couldn't get away with any mischief,\" describing pervasive staff surveillance; square does not describe persistent, day-to-day adult monitoring of student behavior in the same way.",
  "square offers a wider variety of extracurricular clubs and unusual sports than circle": "Square lists many distinct offerings: \"buildOn\", \"the school newspaper, debate club\", \"ice hockey\", \"swimming\" and many AP/advanced courses; circle mentions sports and AP/dual credit but not the same breadth of clubs or unusual sports."
}"]

  "square reports frequent failures to discipline or notify parents about student misconduct more than circle": "Square gives multiple concrete incidents where misbehavior was not appropriately addressed or communicated: 'My son... got into so much trouble there but never repremended... broke a bus window and was caught smoking at the bus stop and the school didn't follow up with us,' whereas Circle focuses on academics and testing rather than recurrent unaddressed student misconduct.",

["{
  "circle offers formal, structured college preparation programs more than square": "Circle: multiple reviewers cite AP, Honors, Dual Enrollment and college visits — e.g., “Both kids entered AP & Honors classes in 9th grade,” “The school offers variuos AP and Dual Enrollment programs and college visits.” Square: reviewers mention students applying to University of California campuses but do not describe formal AP/Dual Enrollment program offerings.",

  "circle reports smaller class sizes / lower student to teacher ratio than square": "Circle states “The student to teacher ratio is very low” and repeatedly notes smaller classes and more one-on-one time.   "circle provides school-issued laptops but also documents technology implementation problems while square does not mention device programs": "Circle: reviewers note laptops were issued but problematic — “The laptops that the school gives out are a waste of time and money... he had so many problems with his laptop that he just stopped using it,” and “the laptops impair learning.” Square contains no mention of a device distribution program or technology-related problems.",
  "circle shows active marketing/PR solicitation of positive online reviews while square shows no such practice": "Circle contains a reviewer accusation that the school PR director emailed students asking them to post positive reviews: “Last year my son showed me an email from the school's P.R./Marketing director where she asked students to post positive reviews on this website.” Square includes no mention of school-directed review solicitation or similar marketing tactics.",
  "square has a large immigrant student population and documents inadequate newcomer placement support more than circle": "Square: reviewer states “There is a large Asian immigrant population on campus” and an immigrant student reports poor placement guidance: “I just came from Indonesia... the counselors did not guide me well to the point where I am not supposed to be in the classes I am in right now” and “I didn't know what classes there are.   "square emphasizes a college application culture focused on University of California campuses and lacks proactive support for out-of-state selective private applications compared with circle": "Square: reviewer notes “Majority of students are applying to University of California campuses and NOT out of state highly selective private universities” and pleads “I hope this school will be more proactive to support more students pursuing admission applications to private schools.” Circle emphasizes diverse college-prep pathways (AP, Dual Enrollment, college visits) rather than a single-application culture.",
  "circle documents greater variety of extracurricular, service, and social opportunities than square": "Circle repeatedly lists clubs, sports, community service and social activities: “There was so much for him to do at school through clubs, sports and academics,” “There is a sport, club, course, event, and group of people that tends to every student's needs.” Square comments focus on academics and teacher support and do not similarly enumerate extracurricular breadth.",
  "circle contains explicit reports of ineffective teaching and unprofessional staff behavior that square does not": "Circle includes direct complaints about staff and instruction: “The assistant dean, David Tuschmann, is very unprofessional,” and “He does NOT teach, gives the students a work sheet...   "circle includes at least one strong complaint that graduates felt underprepared for college after paying substantial tuition, a concern not raised in square": "Circle: a reviewer reports an alumni perspective: “Now in college, my son has said that SJV did not prepare him properly.   "square reports a harmful schedule change (block to period) affecting instruction more than circle": "Square explicitly blames 'recent change back to a Period system instead of a block schedule' for cramming content and poorer retention: 'Students are now crammed with so much info in one day that there is no way they will be able to retain it properly'; circle does not describe schedule-policy changes harming instruction.",

  "circle describes explicit administrative priorities on fundraising and athletics over classroom improvements while square emphasizes administrative policy failure in academics": "Circle criticizes the principal's fundraising priorities—'principal only cares about getting more and more funds' applied to visible athletic/facility projects rather than classrooms—whereas square emphasizes that 'The administration has failed to enact proficient policies that encourage students to try their best in school,' framing the administration failure in terms of academic policy and oversight.",
  "circle reports socioeconomic bias in scholarship allocation disadvantaging middle class more than square": "Circle warns 'If you are middle class, be ready to pay full tuition. You have to be poor or in sports to get the good scholarships,' a specific equity issue not mentioned in square.",
  "circle reports a faith based, family oriented educational mission and associated spiritual programming more than square": "Circle repeatedly frames itself as a faith-based, nurturing community—'faith-based, college-preparatory education', 'Swordsman family', 'developed my academic skills and spiritually'—whereas square contains no evidence of a religious or faith-based mission shaping curriculum or community."
}"]

["{
  "circle has more specialized advanced academic programs and tracks than square": "Circle repeatedly names multiple advanced offerings—IB (including a ‘wall-to-wall’ IB program), the 7th–8th Academic Center, AVID, ROTC, honors, AP, and dual credit—(e.g. “IB Program For All…”, “Academic Center… 7th and 8th grade program”, “IB, AVID, ROTC… Honors or AP or dual credit”), whereas Square contains no mention of such specialized academic tracks and instead complains about a lack of programs.",
  "circle shows stronger documented student academic outcomes and college placement than square": "Circle provides measurable outcomes like ‘Last year’s average [IB] score was 25.1’ and ‘Last year 98% of the students were accepted to college,’ plus AC students placing at Northside/Payton/Lane; Square offers no comparable outcome statistics or success indicators.",
  "circle has more extensive extracurricular and comprehensive sports offerings than square": "Circle explicitly states broad extracurricular strength and unique sports coverage—‘Taft is the only CPS school to offer 100% of the available sports programs’ and praises theater, music, national travel for teams—while Square only references sports in the sense that ‘If you want a school where sports is most important… then you are looking for Yoakum,’ implying athletics emphasis but not variety or comprehensive offerings.",
  "circle reports significant overcrowding and capacity mismatch more than square": "Circle cites concrete capacity figures and overcrowding problems—‘the school was built for 2400 and… will… have over 3000 students,’ ‘1000 more students than they are equipped for,’ and ‘halls are so bottle necked’—whereas Square does not mention enrollment capacity or overcrowding.",
  "circle reports frequent substance use and lax security incidents (drugs, bathroom smoking) more than square": "Circle repeatedly documents substance-related problems and lax security—‘Drugs, fights… smoking in the bathrooms is obscene’, ‘kids using a hookah pen(in class)’, and ‘security guards aren’t really doing their jobs’—while Square’s safety complaints focus on bullying and administrative priorities rather than substance use or bathroom smoking.",
  "square reports more explicit lack of computers and technology resources than circle": "Square directly asks ‘Where are the computers in this school??’ and argues money is being misallocated away from technology, whereas Circle mentions ‘resources are limited and very old’ but does not explicitly single out missing computer/technology resources.",
  "square reports teacher turnover and perceived staffing quality decline more than circle": "Square foregrounds staff turnover as a core concern—‘why do teachers seem to leave and we end up having more uneducated ones take their place?’—whereas Circle mentions some teachers needing to retire and layoffs but pairs that with multiple praises of ‘teachers that care’ and examples of dedicated staff, making turnover a less central theme.",
  "square reports administrative focus on student dress code over academic supports more than circle": "Square criticizes a new principal who ‘only seems to have concern for what Kids wear’ and urges stakeholders to prioritize academic programs instead, while Circle’s administrative critiques are about responsiveness, registration logistics, or praise for a proactive principal rather than a narrow dress-code focus.",
  "circle reports active alumni and community engagement and fundraising more than square": "Circle contains direct accounts of alumni involvement and foundation/fundraising efforts—‘I have organized many tribute concerts… I have returned to help my Alma Mater,’ and mentions of LSC, PTSA and the Taft High School Foundation—whereas Square calls for parent/faculty/superintendent collaboration but gives no evidence of existing alumni or organized community fundraising activity.",
  "circle reports operational and administrative logistical failures (registration lines, phone unresponsiveness) more than square": "Circle gives concrete operational failures—‘We were at the school for 3 hours waiting to get her schedule… The person in the box office is the slowest… You call the Office, No one answers the phone, you leave a message and no one calls back’—whereas Square’s administrative complaints concern priorities and program funding rather than these specific logistical breakdowns.",
  "square reports daily bullying incidents more than circle": "Square states plainly ‘If you want a school where your child can get bullied on the daily basis then you are in the right place,’ making bullying a central, daily safety issue; Circle includes reports of fights and bullying-like behavior but does not present daily bullying as the primary, recurring problem in the same direct way."
}"]

  "square emphasizes advanced AP/honors offerings and college-prep outcomes more than circle, often alongside unequal access": "Square repeatedly highlights AP/honors success and college readiness (\"Both my children graduated with over a 4.0... received scholarship money,\" \"AP chemistry and AP physics... gave him an advantage in college classes\"), but these comments are paired with concerns about unequal access; Circle makes no mention of AP/honors programs.",

  "circle exhibits a closer, community-oriented school culture and continuity more than square": "Circle emphasizes relational continuity and closeness: \"Everyone is so close!\" and \"I have been going to Indian creek schools since kindergarten,\" while Square repeatedly describes students \"fall[ing] through the cracks\" in a very large institution and says \"It is easy to get lost in a school the size of Pinnacle.\"",
  "square prioritizes athletics funding and support over other departments (for example the arts) more than circle": "Square explicitly claims \"the art department solely relying on the paycheck of its teachers\" while \"this school focuses attention on its sports department as it is the only department that can bring in funding,\" indicating an athletics-first funding priority not present in Circle.",

["{
  "circle reports stronger administrative strictness and higher academic expectations than square": "Circle explicitly states “The administration is extreamly strict” and “Expectations for this school are also very, very high,” whereas Square praises challenging classes but does not describe the school as administratively strict or disciplinarian.",
  "circle requires more parent involvement and mandatory/extra fees than square": "Circle warns “this school requires parent involvement” and that “the school WILL ask you for extra money…Maverick Games…is $100” and a “schoolwide non-optional raffle,” while Square contains no mention of mandatory fundraising or high parent-subsidy requirements.",
  "circle emphasizes active fine arts and athletics programs that take students off campus more than square": "Circle repeatedly praises band, fine arts and coaches who “constantly take us out of that school on trips, competitions, sports events,” a level of organized external activity not described in Square (Square praises a “fantastic music program” but gives no detail about frequent trips/representative travel).",
  "square demonstrates clearer evidence of AP/IB and college preparation outcomes than circle": "Square states the curriculum “more than prepared them for college” and that students “started college the equivalent of sophomores with the AP and IB classes taken,” while Circle contains mixed claims about college prep (some say ‘not really college prep’ or standards are inconsistently applied).",
  "circle contains reports of extreme racist threats and violent racial language more explicitly than square": "Circle reports severe incidents: “I’m black and I've been called the N word multiple times and threatened to be lynched,” language and explicit violent threats that are not present in Square’s accounts.",
  "square reports administrative mishandling of racial incidents and punitive bias toward victims more than circle": "Square relates that a minority student’s administration response effectively rebuked the victim: “the administration has practically endorsed it by punishing my kid's negative reaction to racial slurs much harsher than the instigators,” a specific claim of institutional bias not asserted in Circle.",
  "circle documents bureaucratic scheduling and guidance unresponsiveness and fee barriers more than square": "Circle recounts a placement/scheduling failure and a $100 charge to change classes: “I chose journalism… I got neither… they told me to wait… I have heard no response… if I would like to change to another class it cost 100,” whereas Square specifically praises a guidance counselor who “saved my life,” showing more individualized guidance support.",
  "circle reports higher teacher turnover than square": "Circle explicitly states “High teacher turn-over rate,” a staffing instability not mentioned in Square’s reviews.",
  "square reports more physical student-on-student violence and injuries being ignored than circle": "Square describes severe physical assaults: “I was taunted, jumped by other students to the point of injury and being bloodied,” and says administrators did little, while Circle focuses more on cliques, drugs, and insults rather than repeated accounts of students being physically injured at school.",
  "square highlights systemic neglect where students fall through the cracks more than circle": "Square opens with “I watched as many students were falling through the cracks” and details ongoing ignored problems (drug use, bullies, lack of respect), framing a pattern of neglected vulnerable students; Circle criticizes many things but frames problems more as strictness, cliques, or isolated misconduct rather than a broad pattern of students left unsupported.",
  "circle emphasizes institutional focus on morality, discipline, and religious identity more than square": "Multiple Circle reviews state “Morality and discipline is given a lot of importance” and tout Catholic identity and discipline as central, while Square contains no comparable emphasis on institutional morality or religious formation.",
  "circle reports explicit financial and enrollment access barriers tied to school participation more than square": "Circle warns of non-optional paid events and fundraising and implies socioeconomic sorting—“everyone sending their kid here does it because they want the best for their child and are willing to sacrifice to get it”—whereas Square does not mention cost barriers or mandatory paid activities."
}"]

["{
  "circle emphasizes Catholic / faith-based identity and formation more than square": "Circle repeatedly flags a Catholic mission and faith formation: reviewers say “make sure your son is catholic,” call it a “Catholic environment,” highlight the motto “Men for Others,” and describe deliberate character and moral formation as a backbone of the school, whereas Square includes no mention of religious identity or faith-based programming.",
  "circle enforces stricter, more punitive discipline practices than square": "Circle describes a rigid detention policy where “If you do anything … you get detention” and detentions include writing poems, scripts and copybooks, and reviewers call the “discipline policy is the worst”; Square reports disciplinary problems (fights, threats) but not a pervasive, codified punitive detention system described in Circle.",
  "square reports more pervasive inconsistent or poor classroom instruction than circle": "Square contains many explicit claims that “many teachers don't do their jobs,” “Most of the teachers can't teach,” and numerous examples of teachers being inattentive or inexperienced, while Circle’s criticisms of teachers are limited to isolated comments like “some of the teachers are mean and/or rude” or “aside from his English teacher, all of the teachers are fair.”",
  "circle is described as selective and admission-competitive more than square": "Circle states “It is a competitive process to get in to JHS” and describes higher expectations for admitted students, whereas Square is discussed as a large zoned public high school where reviewers repeatedly describe it as what you make of it and tied to neighborhood zoning rather than selective admissions.",
  "circle frames community service and character development as institutional priorities more than square": "Circle explicitly says “Community service is an extremely important component” and that forming “men for others” is the backbone of the education, while Square's reviews emphasize extracurricular opportunities and academics but do not describe community service or moral formation as central institutional priorities.",
  "square documents more failures in special education identification and accommodations than circle": "Square includes a detailed account that the district “refused to test her,” reports denial of accommodations (refusing to grade a dyslexic student), and describes hiring advocates and attorneys; Circle contains no comparable accounts of special education testing failures or accommodation denials.",
  "square reports more safety incidents and visible student behavior problems than circle": "Square reviewers mention “bomb threats/fights/gangs” and students not wanting to finish school there due to safety, whereas Circle’s entries focus on discipline, academics and character with no reports of bomb threats, gangs, or similar campus-safety incidents.",
  "circle contains more explicit complaints about unequal enforcement and favoritism than square": "Circle explicitly accuses the school of unequal discipline and exceptions for certain people—“discipline is not equal (depending on who you are) … exceptions made for certain people” and calls out a coach as “extremely partial,” while Square's criticisms center on variable teaching and administration rather than documented favoritism in enforcement.",
  "square highlights broader large-school extracurricular breadth and strong fine arts programs more than circle": "Square repeatedly praises a wide array of offerings—“variety of clubs and honors programs,” “fine arts program is fantastic,” and a strong band/theater presence—whereas Circle highlights particular clubs (debate, environmental) and sports but emphasizes a tighter brotherhood and fewer distinct program areas.",
  "circle reports institutional grading rigor that may lower GPA relative to public schools more than square": "Circle warns that the school “does not 'pad' the grades like the public schools do” so “when it is time to apply for college your GPA is not as high as the public school students,” a specific institutional grading practice affecting college admissions; Square instead focuses on AP versus regular class rigor and does not describe the school intentionally avoiding grade inflation.",
  "square portrays more administrative dysfunction and poor parent communication than circle": "Square contains several examples of administrative/communication failures—parents unable to stop automated calls, an inexperienced principal allegedly imposing experimental methods, and complaints of cold office staff—while Circle’s only administrative critique is a request that the guidance department needs an overhaul, with otherwise frequent praise of leadership.",
  "circle is described as an all-boys single-sex environment while square is described as a coeducational public high school": "Circle repeatedly frames the student body as boys/men—reviewers refer to “son,” “young men,” and “they come in as boys … they leave as men”—whereas Square refers to sons and daughters, multiple families with both genders, and large coed programming across academics and extracurriculars."
}"]

["{
  "circle shows more administrative unresponsiveness and dismissiveness than square": "Multiple circle reviews describe administrators as uncaring or dismissive—e.g. the assistant principal told a parent \"That is the discretion of the teacher if the students do not want to listen do not want to listen\" and reviewers call the principal and assistant principal \"disgraces\" or \"heartless.\" In square, reviewers repeatedly thank LHS staff and say \"Awesome Teachers\" and \"Thank you LHS teachers, staff,\" with only minor complaints about favoritism, not systemic administrator indifference.",
  "circle shows more widespread student misconduct and schoolwide discipline problems than square": "Circle repeatedly reports unruly, disrespectful students and declining behavior—\"students are unruly, disrespectful\" and \"students goofing off and talking\" during class; several reviewers say the school \"has gotten worse with each passing year.\" Square mentions a \"few trouble makers\" and suggests tougher discipline but otherwise describes a generally positive environment like \"overall a pretty good school.\"",
  "circle shows more unchecked bullying and safety concerns than square": "Circle explicitly states \"Bullying runs rampant and unchecked by the staff\" and gives an example where an admitted threat \"still went unchecked,\" whereas square contains no sustained claims of pervasive bullying and instead highlights community support and safety, e.g. \"People rally around each other in time of need.\"",
  "circle shows more exam and assessment quality problems than square": "Circle complaints include \"Final exams are a joke\" and that study guides were \"no more than cheat sheets with fill in the blanks and used during exams,\" while square emphasizes honors classes and students getting into college without any allegations of weak or invalid assessments.",
  "circle shows more failures in special education and attendance accommodation processes than square": "Circle reviewers complain specifically that \"Their 504/IEP sucks!\" and that the \"attendance lady will not accept notes half the time signed by a doctor,\" whereas square has only one isolated complaint about a student with a baby whose \"home tutor teachers refuse to give tutor work and no communication,\" not a pattern about 504/IEP or attendance processing.",
  "circle shows more restrictive or punitive daily policies affecting students (for example hydration rules) than square": "Circle mentions strict rules harming daily needs—\"They cant even have water in class. Ok so all these athletes can just dehydrate.....they dont care.\" Square does not report similarly strict campus policies limiting basic student needs.",
  "circle shows higher teacher turnover and staffing instability than square": "Circle reviews note \"teachers coming and going left and right\" and \"we have lost a lot of teachers because they do not agree with the choices of the administration,\" whereas square repeatedly praises long-term staff and alumni-teacher continuity (\"I had great teachers,\" \"awesome teachers\").",
  "square shows stronger honors offerings and demonstrable college/athletic progression outcomes than circle": "Square explicitly references \"honors classes,\" and outcomes such as \"I got into my college of choice\" and \"graduated last year and now play soccer in college,\" while circle contains complaints that learning happens mostly in honors/AP and fewer concrete success stories about college placement.",
  "square shows more community cohesion and mutual support than circle": "Square reviewers describe a \"wonderful community feel\" where \"people rally around each other in time of need,\" whereas circle contains multiple reports of exclusivity and parents/students feeling unwelcome—\"It has become a very exclusive school and if you aren't in the clique you're not welcome.\"",
  "circle highlights strong niche extracurriculars like JROTC and drill team more than square does": "Several circle reviewers single out JROTC and the drill team as \"one of the best programs\" and \"outstanding,\" while square emphasizes broader arts and sports opportunities but does not repeatedly single out JROTC/drill as a distinctive strength.",
  "square highlights arts programming more than circle": "Square explicitly notes \"I do like the fact that there are Arts opportunities available as well as sports,\" and multiple reviewers praise theater and arts involvement, whereas circle's recurring extracurricular praise centers more on JROTC, drill team, and certain sports rather than arts.",
  "circle shows worse classroom-level management by teachers than square": "Circle contains a direct classroom recording example where a teacher continued lecturing through two phone rings and 15 minutes of students \"goofing off and talking\" without regaining control—\"the teacher never missed a beat with her lecture or tried to regain any control.\" Square contains no comparable examples of teachers failing to manage classroom behavior and several statements praising teachers as \"caring and helpful.\"",
  "circle reports more social exclusivity and clique culture affecting parents and students than square": "Circle reviewers explicitly say the school \"has become a very exclusive school\" and \"if you aren't in the clique you're not welcome there,\" while square acknowledges some favoritism for those who \"know someone\" but otherwise emphasizes inclusivity and community support."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports classroom teaching methods and teacher responsiveness more than square": "Circle includes concrete classroom-level examples about pedagogy and teacher behavior, e.g. parents complained a teacher's \"refusal to grade homework & use it as a learning tool, showing videos in class & refusing to provide more than two or three examples during a class period,\" and statements like \"Many of the Marian teachers seem like they teach for money\"; Square contains no classroom- or instruction-level detail.",
  "circle describes student social climate and peer behavior more than square": "Circle repeatedly documents peer dynamics and social problems such as \"a lot of cliques and spoiled brats,\" \"students are spoiled rich kids who think they are better than everyone,\" and mentions social harms like \"has damaged her self esteem,\" whereas Square focuses exclusively on district governance and mentions no student peer climate.",
  "circle details academic programs and student support services more than square": "Circle names specific academic offerings and supports — \"AP/Honors,\" \"well-trained counselors, tutors, and a student success coordinator\" — describing concrete services that prepare students; Square does not describe any school-level programs, courses, or support staff.",
  "circle reports religious identity and faith programming while square does not": "Circle explicitly frames the school as parochial with statements like \"I came from a catholic grade school,\" \"The faith life at Marian is outstanding,\" and \"I ABSOLUTLY have become a holier person,\" indicating active faith programming; Square contains no reference to religious identity or faith-based programming.",
  "circle discusses tuition and private versus public tradeoffs more than square": "Circle includes explicit commentary about cost and choice: \"You pay almost $10,000 every year for an education you could get at a public school for free,\" and mentions parents choosing OPS/public schools for teacher quality; Square instead focuses on public district budgeting but does not discuss tuition or private/public family tradeoffs.",
  "circle asserts concrete student academic outcomes and college preparation more than square": "Circle offers outcome claims such as students being \"well prepared for college\" and one student being placed \"in the drivers seat for a full ride to a one of the best schools in the country,\" while Square makes no claims about student academic outcomes or college readiness.",
  "circle highlights teacher motivation, tenure, and enforcement of teaching standards more than square": "Circle criticizes long-tenured teachers and enforcement, e.g. \"This school is expensive... and yet does not enforce good teaching standards for long time teachers\" and suggests teachers feel secure through the \"parochial school system,\" whereas Square does not discuss teacher tenure or internal personnel standards.",
  "square centers on district fiscal management and calls for budget transparency more than circle": "Square is explicitly about finances and governance: \"The budget expenses for the past decade should be analyzed and made public\" and \"Demand fiscal accountability!\"; Circle, by contrast, contains no allegation about district-level fiscal mismanagement or calls for public budget analysis.",
  "square alleges poor governance decision making and lack of integrity more than circle": "Square accuses administrators and the school committee of failing children and lacking honesty: \"administrators, including the school committee are not making well informed decisions for all of our children based on principles of integrity and honesty,\" while Circle focuses on classroom, social, programmatic, and faith issues rather than committee-level integrity.",
  "circle describes single sex schooling and its classroom impact while square does not": "Circle explicitly notes single-sex benefits: \"No worry about how the boys will see you so you can actually focus on your education,\" indicating the school's single-sex environment affects student experience; Square contains no discussion of single-sex schooling or its effects.",
  "circle documents mixed academic fit and selective success for certain students more than square": "Circle contains contrasting reports that the school \"provides a great environment for a female to learn\" and that it is right for those \"academically driven,\" alongside accounts of students who struggled and were advised to drop classes, showing variability in fit and selectivity; Square offers a single systemic critique and gives no evidence on student fit or selectivity."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports more frequent physical fights, fire alarm pulling, and thefts than square": "Circle repeatedly describes physical disorder: “All the student do is pull the fire alarm and fight outside,” and several thefts are described (“My friend got her phone stolen on the first day,” “Junior year someone stole my daughter iPhone”), whereas Square contains no reports of fights, alarms, or theft incidents.",
  "circle describes a less effective security presence and weaker incident response than square": "Circle states security and staff failed to resolve incidents: “Security seemed to be in place, but I don't think they worked very hard in helping me solve that issue,” and “administrators do not report violent episodes,” while Square explicitly says the school has “a very involved principal and excellent teachers,” indicating more effective staff involvement.",
  "circle reports administrative negligence and pressure to pass students more than square": "Circle claims administrators ignore problems and pressure passing: “They blame the teachers and demand that we pass students who do not go to class” and “Parents of current students should file suit against CPS for allowing an incompetent individual to run a school,” whereas Square praises administrative leadership: “a very involved principal.”",
  "square emphasizes stronger advanced course availability and college matriculation outcomes than circle": "Square states “DHS offers so many AP classes” and “My son and his friends were all admitted to great colleges/universities,” while Circle frames the school as one with “low test scores and overall grade” and only mentions future program changes (IB) rather than current breadth of AP/college-prep success.",
  "square reports more caring, actively involved teachers guiding students than circle": "Square: “his teachers were actively involved and offered him excellent guidance” and “His teachers were very caring,” whereas Circle describes teachers who ‘just don't care’ to an extent and relies on a few teachers to contact parents because administration ignored issues.",
  "circle reports pervasive bullying, targeted harassment, and student-on-student victimization more than square": "Circle details repeated bullying and targeted thefts leading to transfers and fear: “my son was bullied at Bogan,” “my cousin had to transfer out because she was constantly teased and was always bullied,” and students “were jumped on… got her book bag, ipod 3g, and cellphone taken,” while Square contains no accounts of bullying or targeted victimization.",
  "circle reports evidence of grade inflation or students passing without attendance more than square": "Circle claims students “can actually sit in class and do nothing and get a passing grade” and that administrators “put so much pressure on the teachers to pass a student,” whereas Square describes students being challenged and guided in rigorous AP classes.",
  "square reports students having meaningful control of academic pathways and individualized guidance more than circle": "Square: “My son was in control of his academic experience, but his teachers were actively involved and offered him excellent guidance,” indicating student agency plus supports, a dynamic absent from Circle’s accounts of disrupted classrooms and lack of instructional continuity.",
  "circle documents community reputation and historical decline alongside plans for structural program change more than square": "Circle situates the school as a struggling neighborhood school with “low test scores,” nostalgia about past decades (“in the 80's it was one of the best…I graduated in 1988”), and imminent structural change (“Bogan is going wall to wall IB”), while Square focuses on current strengths and does not narrate historical decline or major program overhauls.",
  "circle explicitly links lack of extracurricular and sports offerings to student misconduct more than square": "Circle argues the school “needs more sports teams and activities to keep many students occupied and motivated and out of trouble,” framing extracurricular scarcity as a driver of misbehavior; Square mentions limited extracurricular options (“the amount offered is limited”) but frames them as an area for improvement rather than a proximate cause of disorder."
}"]

["{

  "square reports widespread and ongoing bullying and safety problems whereas circle does not report bullying": "Square repeatedly reports bullying and fights as persistent problems: “bullying goes unchecked,” “As a student going there now, I'm bullied daily,” and “fights happen more than they should,” whereas Circle contains no descriptions of bullying or safety incidents at the school.",

  "square reports significantly weaker college preparation in math and sciences whereas circle claims the school prepares students for the future": "Square notes concrete academic outcomes: “I was inadequately prepared in most aareas, especially math and sciences” and “My son is in college, and he is struggling with mathematics and science,” while Circle asserts the school “fully prepares students for the future” and highlights graduates continuing education successfully.",

  "circle reports consistently strong teacher quality and student support whereas square reports many teachers who do not teach or who act uncaring or bullying": "Circle contains multiple endorsements of staff: “The teachers, coaches, and staff are fantastic,” “She always had support and guidance from numerous teachers and staff,” whereas Square includes accusations such as “most teachers do not teach,” “teachers themselves act like bullies,” and “This school treated me like I was stupid.”",

  "circle reports active inclusion efforts and character development whereas square claims the school prioritizes sports and grades over true learning and inclusion": "Circle praises inclusive outreach and character work: “The principal has done a great job involving all students… creating focus on integrity and character development,” whereas Square criticizes priorities: “They focus mainly on sports and good grades, not if the students are learning anything.”",

  "circle reports resolution of past leadership problems through staff turnover whereas square attributes decline to past superintendents with unresolved consequences": "Circle notes that previously problematic administrators “has gone elsewhere; same is true of a particularly inept curriculum coordinator,” suggesting turnover fixed issues, while Square blames leadership changes for decline—“We can thank the previous superintendent for this!”—and continues to report ongoing problems, implying unresolved harm.",

  "circle describes consistently positive extracurricular staff involvement whereas square describes program-specific strong pockets (music) but inconsistent support elsewhere": "Circle praises extracurricular personnel broadly: “The teachers, coaches, and staff are fantastic,” whereas Square gives a mixed picture—strong support in the music program (“the music department was like a second family”) but otherwise reports uneven student support and recurring problems in other areas."

    "circle reports at least one functioning extracurricular (band) while square reports minimal clubs and low school spirit": "Circle specifically notes “The band is pretty good though,” indicating a working music program, whereas Square complains “the clubs and activities are minimal” and that the school “doesn't have enough school spirit.”",
    "circle depicts punitive administration enforcing rules whereas square includes claims of supportive faculty and mentorship": "Circle emphasizes harsh administrative action by naming the principal's role in long suspensions for dress-code violations; Square directly states that “the faculty and staff are the most supportive mentors I have ever had,” indicating stronger classroom-level support in some accounts.",
    "square shows high internal inconsistency in student experience (both severe bullying/exclusion and strong academic/supportive reports) while circle focuses on a single systemic discipline problem": "Square contains conflicting reviewer claims within the same entry — one accuses the school of being a “popularity contest” with bullying that forced students to leave, while another praises rigorous academics and supportive staff and describes personal college success. Circle's account centers on a single, concrete systemic issue (discriminatory suspensions and the resulting federal lawsuit) rather than contrasting portrayals of day-to-day experience."
}"]

  "circle reports district funding mismatches and visible administrative perks more than square": "Circle notes spending contradictions: despite limited funds for basic services, \"they can afford to send the higher up administration around on five golf carts\" and \"spend unneeded amounts of money on sports events.\" Square criticizes responsiveness and privilege but does not depict this specific misallocation of district resources.",
  "circle reports a one to one laptop program and focused technology education more than square": "Circle states a concrete technology offering: \"Each student gets a laptop to use for the school year as well as a lot of education on technology.\" Square does not mention a 1:1 laptop program or equivalent technology initiative.",
  "circle reports categorical tracking and student placement practices more than square": "Circle documents specific tracking and misplacement: \"I was always put in the class with troubled students, while the 'gifted' students were recognized and placed in a 'special' class\" and \"The school system liked to categorize students based on last name.\" Square criticizes cliques and favoritism but does not describe systemic tracking by ability or administrative sorting by last name.",
  "circle reports inconsistently enforced or contradictory local policies more than square": "Circle gives concrete examples of policy contradictions and inconsistent enforcement: the no idling rule is enforced yet parents parking to avoid idling are reprimanded—\"If you idle you get yelled at... park so that you do not waste all of your gas IDLING they do not like that either.\" Square criticizes administration broadly but does not offer this kind of specific policy-contradiction example.",

}"]

  "circle provides organized orientation and knowledgeable student led campus tours while square does not": "Circle describes a concrete onboarding practice: \"After orientation, Anna, our senior tour guide, showed our son the entire campus and was very knowledgeable and kind,\" while Square contains no mention of formal orientation or student-guided tours.",
