["{
  "circle portrays broader inclusivity and transformative support for students regardless of starting point whereas square conditions success on pre-existing responsibility": "Circle states the school “takes kids where they are at academically and socially and transforms them into productive members of society,” implying support for a wide range of students; Square says success is conditional: “So if your child is dedicated and already responsible with their time ... this would be a good recommendation,” which frames success as dependent on students' prior discipline.",
  "square exhibits lax discipline and inconsistent enforcement leading to rule favoritism, circle does not": "Square documents concrete disciplinary problems: “teachers allow children to continue to turn in assignment weeks and sometimes months after it was due,” “Disciplinary action is also very lacking,” and “If you get on the good side of the faculty you can break a good chunk of the rules,” whereas Circle makes no mention of weak enforcement or favoritism.",
  "square documents strong competitive extracurricular programs and consistent state championships, circle does not": "Square lists specific programs and outcomes: “My kids ... are in activities such as orchestra, science olympiad, and film club” and “Students in science olympiad, forensics, and music, as well as athletics, are state champions every year,” while Circle offers no comparable catalog of extracurricular offerings or championship-level outcomes.",
  "square reports availability of college-credit courses and certificates whereas circle does not": "Square notes concrete academic offerings that carry external credentialing: “you also get a few certificates and college credits if you pick the correct classes,” a specific programmatic feature not mentioned in Circle.",
  "square highlights measurable academic outcomes despite socioeconomic challenges (≈40% free/reduced meals and above-average test scores) whereas circle does not": "Square provides a socioeconomic and outcome datapoint: “40% of students get free and reduced price meals, having above-average test scores is pretty impressive,” linking measurable test performance to the student population; Circle does not reference socioeconomic composition or comparative test outcomes.",
  "square reports social cliques as a notable problem in the student body whereas circle does not": "Square explicitly identifies peer-group division: “the school has many cliques which in my opinion is also detrimental to the school,” while Circle makes no mention of clique-related social fragmentation.",
  "square links lenient grading/assignment policies to reduced college readiness whereas circle does not": "Square connects policy to downstream outcomes: allowing late work “might cause the school to look like it's getting great grades but it also causes deceleration of student readiness for college making it a hard transition,” a specific causal concern not raised in Circle.",
  "circle emphasizes coordinated teacher and administrator teamwork driving school quality more than square, which highlights individual leaders and uneven staff practices": "Circle foregrounds a unified staff: “This school has a dedicated team of teachers and administrators,” presenting joint effort as the driver of quality; Square praises the principal and committed teachers but also describes uneven practices (discipline, favoritism), framing leadership and staff quality as more mixed and person-dependent.",
  "circle stresses that school quality should be judged beyond simple metrics more than square, which emphasizes measurable achievements and awards": "Circle asserts a philosophical stance: “A school's greatness cannot be measured by simple metrics,” focusing on holistic development; Square repeatedly cites measurable indicators—state championships, above-average test scores, college credits—as evidence of the school's strengths."
}"]

["{
  "square reports frequent student violence, bullying, and theft incidents whereas circle does not": "Square contains multiple concrete accounts of unsafe student behavior: “the kids there are so mean... on the last day of school there was a huge fight and rung the bell early,” and “people are always stealing things, even little things like a wallet.” Circle contains no reports of fights, bullying, or theft.",
  "square reports lack of instructional resources (no books, few computers) while circle does not mention resource shortfalls": "Square states explicit resource shortages: “There are no books, very few computers,” and reviewers note the school “wastes what resources it does get.” Circle makes no mention of library, textbook, or computer shortages.",
  "circle identifies a specifically weak math program while square criticizes general instructional methods without singling out math": "Circle directly says “Their math program is very weak.” Square criticizes pedagogy broadly — e.g. “most of the teaching comes from students reading the book out loud and then doing the problems at the end of the chapter” — but does not single out math as the specific weak subject.",
  "circle highlights strong competitive extracurricular programs whereas square contains little or mixed praise for extracurriculars": "Circle praises extracurriculars: “Their sports, dance, and band are very good and competitive.” Square includes very little consistent praise for athletics/arts and focuses on other operational and climate issues, with only scattered positive comments about specific staff or student initiative.",
  "square reports broader staff and office unprofessionalism and administrative dysfunction while circle only notes uneven teacher email responsiveness": "Square details unprofessional behavior across staff and admin: “The office staff has no manners, very inconsiderate, loud, obnoxious, rude,” principals “was yelling,” and reviewers call for administrative replacement; circle only mentions uneven teacher communication: “Some teachers will respond to emails, while others do not.”",
  "square reports favoritism in discipline and inconsistent enforcement of rules whereas circle notes limited options for struggling students but not favoritism": "Square alleges disciplinary double standards: “Their is a high amount of favoritism if a student participates in more activities then the punishment of their actions are lowered,” and describes inconsistent rule enforcement by principals; circle instead reports limited recourse for students who struggle with a teacher: “There are few options if your child does not do well with the teacher.”",
  "square documents administrative turnover and change over time whereas circle presents a single static snapshot": "Square contains time-based observations and comparisons: “since we have gotten new principals everything is not the same anymore,” and multiple reviewers reference improvement under a “new administrative team,” indicating change over years. Circle gives a single contemporaneous assessment with no temporal narrative.",
  "square documents contentious graduation logistics and ticket limitations while circle makes no mention of graduation practices": "Square includes concrete complaints about graduation ticket policy and fundraising: reviewers say the school “cannot afford to give students more than 4 tickets for graduation” and argue the school denied chances to raise funds or purchase extra tickets; circle does not mention graduation procedures or event logistics.",
  "square includes reports of teachers willing to help and student initiative while circle emphasizes lack of options for struggling students": "Within square some reviewers say teachers “are more then willing to help out the students” and note student initiative: “I am impressed with how the students take their own initiative for their education.” Circle, by contrast, highlights limited alternatives for students who don’t fit with a teacher: “There are few options if your child does not do well with the teacher.”"
}"]

["{
  "circle has more boarding/dorm program presence and dorm-specific issues than square": "Circle repeatedly references boarding and dorm life (e.g., “He is a boarder… he has been welcomed,” and later “The dorm program is poorly run”), including both positive welcome experiences and explicit operational problems; Square contains no mention of boarding, dorms, or residential life.",
  "circle has a stronger sports-oriented culture and long daily athletes' hours than square": "Multiple Circle reviews emphasize athletics driving the student schedule and time commitment (e.g., “If playing sports, my son is truly gone from 6:30am until 7:30pm,” and “This is a very sports oriented school”); Square makes no comparable claim about a dominating athletic culture.",
  "circle shows greater socioeconomic selection and wealth-focused social hierarchy than square": "Circle contains many claims linking social status and wealth to student treatment and culture (e.g., “Many people think that Bolles is only a place for 'rich brats'… Money and who has it is at the forefront,” “the school places a heavy emphasis on a families socio-economic status”); by contrast Square highlights diversity and community and does not describe wealth-based social gatekeeping.",
  "circle reports admissions practices evaluating family economic status more than square": "Circle reviewers describe admissions staff questioning careers/neighborhoods and implying economic evaluation (e.g., “the admissions representative… questioned my husband and I about our careers, what neighborhood we were considering,” and recommending coordinating with the Dean of Admissions for diversity); Square contains no reports of admissions evaluating families’ socioeconomic standing.",
  "circle has heavier academic workload and more frequent AP/honors course emphasis than square": "Circle reviewers explicitly describe substantial rigor and homework load (e.g., “There is SO much homework… Many AP classes,” “the rigor at Bolles is substantially beyond the best the public schools have to offer”); Square praises core academics but does not emphasize excessive homework or heavy AP/honors load.",
  "circle reports more bullying, cliquishness, and minority-targeted mistreatment than square": "Circle contains multiple accounts of cliquey social atmosphere and targeted mistreatment (e.g., “The school along with the families promote a cliquey environment and favor their own people, it gets even worse for minorities,” “picked on by the teachers… ripped out my child’s self-esteem”), whereas Square’s criticisms are limited to teacher favoritism and a single parent remark about decline without the same pattern of minority-targeted abuse.",
  "circle reports more variability in teacher quality and willingness to help than square": "Circle reviewers repeatedly note a broad spread in teacher effectiveness and availability (e.g., “Many teachers pride themselves on being 'hard'… many teachers are not willing to help,” “The teachers and staff could not be more helpful… [but] some are of the 'teach yourself' variety”); Square emphasizes consistently strong, caring teachers and does not describe that same variability.",
  "circle reports explicit concerns about school policy enforcement and dorm rule disputes more than square": "Circle contains direct debate about enforcement and dorm rules (one reviewer defends enforcement: “Bolles is very adamant about following school policies and they enforce them constantly,” while others say “The dorm program is poorly run” and mention allegations like smoking in dorms); Square includes no discussion of policy enforcement or dorm rule disputes.",
  "circle reports higher tuition and affordability concerns than square": "Circle explicitly calls the school “very expensive tuition” and notes financial sacrifice and desire to send additional children but unable to afford it (“It is a very expensive tuition, but worth every cent,” “My parents gave up a lot to send me to Bolles”); Square contains no commentary about tuition or cost burden.",
  "square reports stronger fine arts programs and long-term community legacy than circle": "Square explicitly highlights strong Fine Arts offerings and institutional longevity (e.g., “The Fine Arts Department (music, art, theater, newspaper) - among the best in the city” and “This school is still going strong 50+ years later”), while Circle’s reviews emphasize athletics and college prep rather than a standout fine arts program.",
  "square reports more consistent positive leadership, security, and school community than circle": "Square reviewers credit principals and the school environment for a positive, secure atmosphere (e.g., “the school principals who are top notch,” “There is a sense of security and community”), whereas Circle shows more mixed evidence about leadership and climate with repeated accounts of cliquishness, variable staff responsiveness, and conflicting reports about dorm management."
}"]

["{
  "circle is more explicitly Christian / faith oriented than square": "Circle repeatedly states the school is 'Christian-based' and describes faith-infused classroom practices — e.g. 'we had us writing Bible scripture as part of our notes for our ethics class' and teaching 'chastity' instead of sex education — while Square contains no mention of religious or faith-based instruction.",
  "circle enforces stricter dress code and uniform policies than square": "Circle repeatedly refers to a strict dress code and its enforcement ('strict dress code, strict dress-code enforcing teachers', 'The uniforms are very ugly'), whereas Square contains no discussion of uniforms or dress-code enforcement.",
  "circle reports more teacher favoritism and 'teacher pet' academic bias than square": "Circle claims teachers 'favor certain students that kiss up to them (teachers pet)' and that favoritism affects attention and outcomes; Square notes athlete-related preferential treatment but does not describe the same classroom-level 'kissing up' favoritism impacting academics.",
  "square shows more athletic-based preferential treatment than circle": "Square explicitly states sports stars receive disproportionate attention ('if you are a sports star you will find you get a lot more attention at this school'), a form of preferential treatment not described in Square's counterparty evidence in Circle which emphasizes teacher/administrative favoritism instead.",
  "circle reports more mishandling of bullying and bigotry by staff than square": "Circle contains multiple allegations of poor handling of harassment and bigotry by staff (e.g. a student forced to write a note that resulted in 'telling him to kill himself', 'Racial slurs... were not uncommon', staff discouraged black students celebrating their culture), while Square mentions harassment and racism but with less detail about staff actively enabling or mishandling incidents.",
  "circle provides abstinence/chastity-focused ethics instruction instead of comprehensive sex education while square does not": "Circle reports ethics classes included writing scripture and teaching 'chastity' rather than 'providing any sort of sex education course or resources regarding safe sex' and links this to student pregnancy concerns; Square contains no similar description of abstinence-focused or absent sex education.",
  "circle reports more frequent hiring of inexperienced or unqualified teachers and resulting instructional gaps than square": "Circle alleges 'a lot of them are new/young teachers and don't know how to help the students who are struggling' and examples of unqualified hires ('a woman with a degree in music education to teach geometry'), while Square acknowledges faculty turnover but also repeatedly praises strong, excellent teachers and rigorous AP classes.",
  "circle highlights strong character-driven athletics leadership and coaching more than square": "Circle contains multiple positive, detailed endorsements of athletic leadership and coaching character (praising the athletic director and varsity coach for leadership and character) whereas Square mentions sports success (e.g., 'Bay Area top 25 basketball team') but focuses more on program results than on character-driven leadership.",
  "square emphasizes small school size and agricultural community context more than circle": "Square opens by warning it is 'a tiny agricultural community barely keeping up with the competitive academic atmosphere of the Bay Area' and ties limited offerings to the community context; Circle reviews do not mention an agricultural, tiny-community context.",
  "square reports underfunded music program and inadequate pool facilities, circle reports different facility problems": "Square explicitly names underfunded music ('The music program... is small and underfunded') and a 'terrible pool', while Circle lists other facility/operations issues (poor lunch quality 'The lunches make kids puke', 'their heaters inside do not work good enough', and complaints about inclement-weather closures) — the specific troubled facilities differ between the two schools.",
  "circle enacts disruptive scheduling/closure policies that disproportionately burden families more than square": "Circle includes complaints about 'Inclement Weather' school closure days being 'out of control' and disruptive for single parents and work schedules ('If you are a single parent trying to keep your job... this is a very real challenge'), while Square's reviews do not raise similar scheduling/closure policy complaints.",
  "circle presents more contradictory extremes of academic reputation and severe instructional deficiencies than square": "Circle's reviews oscillate between strong claims of college-prep excellence ('great academic school... prepares students for a life of success') and reports of inadequate instruction and missing support ('The teachers give the students very little individual attention', 'NEVER heard anything back from them', 'teachers don't know what to do'), whereas Square more consistently frames the school as limited in breadth ('class offerings are slim') but with clearly described strong AP options and successful graduates rather than the same level of coexistence of high praise and severe operational failures."
}"]

["{
  "circle enforces strict uniform and appearance policies more than square": "Circle reviewers cite many appearance rules and punishments: \"if you were missing a flag pin or a year pin you got a detention,\" \"if we didn't have clear book bags we had to carry our books everywhere,\" and \"missing a small piece of your uniform...They'll keep you in disciplined...for the rest of the school day.\" No mention of uniform/appearance enforcement appears in square.",
  "circle uses heavy security and punitive in‑school isolation for discipline whereas square does not describe this": "Circle repeatedly describes militaristic discipline and security: \"bootcamp like mentality for discipline,\" \"useless security,\" and detention rooms described as \"A room with chairs, no windows and awkward silence.\" Square contains no description of security presence or punitive isolation rooms.",
  "circle enrolls a broadly inclusive, high‑needs student population that reviewers link to lower test scores more than square": "Circle notes CAP \"accepts every challenge\" and serves \"AP classes to special ed. for the severely autistic and honors students to returned drop-outs,\" with reviewers explaining \"That's why our PSSA scores are often below average; CAP accepts every challenge.\" Square's critiques focus on policy/practice rather than broadly inclusive enrollment.",
  "square relies heavily on online credit recovery (E2020) to allow failing students to make up large portions of their credit load, which circle does not describe": "Square explicitly warns that \"students are...being allowed to make up more than half their credit load by doing E 2020 classes online.\" No circle review describes extensive online credit recovery as a school practice.",
  "circle shows administrative focus on appearance and strict rule enforcement over academics more than square": "Circle reviewers repeatedly blame administration: \"they are worried more about the appearance of the students,\" \"the administrative of the school care more about tiny details like appearance than the academic quality,\" and \"It is more the administrators fault than the teachers.\" Square instead contains praise that \"leaders continue to push for higher standards for the entire student body.\"",
  "square tolerates chronic absenteeism with little consequence whereas circle describes strict in‑school control of student presence and behavior": "Square complains that \"students are allowed to miss as many days as they please with no consequences even when they get into the 40 and 50 days absent.\" Circle, conversely, emphasizes strict on‑site control (detentions, enforced uniforms, no cutting class) rather than absentee tolerance.",
  "circle reports overcrowded physical circulation and restrictive locker policies more than square": "Circle gives specific space and locker complaints: \"extremely overcrowded hallways...run back and forth in 3 min. in the extremely overcrowded hallways just to get to our lockers,\" and \"they made us pay 10 dollars for a lock...if you didn't get a locker you got a detention.\" Square contains no discussion of overcrowding or locker policies.",
  "circle reports explicit favoritism and unequal treatment of students, while square emphasizes inclusive treatment and support in athletics and classroom advancement": "Circle reviewers charge \"favoritism\" and say \"sport-active students get more attention\" and \"This school only love Hispanic children.\" Square highlights inclusivity: \"She has also been supported to be a part of an athletic team...she is treated as an integral part of the team\" and \"If a child wants to learn they will be supported! If they want to participate they are welcomed!\"",

  "square expresses explicit concern that graduates lack real‑world readiness as a result of district practices more than circle": "Square warns \"Senior students are graduating without real capacity for the world outside of school,\" attributing this to absenteeism and credit recovery; circle reviews instead focus critiques on discipline, administration, and test scores rather than explicit statements about graduates' real‑world readiness."
}"]

["{
  "circle offers specialized arts (VPA) and IB programs more than square": "Circle explicitly describes VPA and IB pathways and strong music departments ('a VPA 9th grader & IB senior', 'All the music departments are fabulous'), whereas Square contains no mention of dedicated arts magnet or IB programming and focuses on general comprehensive high school issues.",
  "circle yields stronger college-preparation outcomes and scholarship success than square": "Circle reviewers report concrete college outcomes ('my son was accepted to OCU with a HUGE scholarship', 'Classen prepared me for college', 'being paid to go to college') and multiple 'A students', while Square cites low rankings and only modest graduation-oriented praise ('ranking of 278/344', 'The school is 3/5... worth going to if your looking to graduate').",
  "circle demonstrates more consistent teacher engagement and active parent/administration involvement than square": "Circle emphasizes parental and administrative involvement ('I am very involved with the administration and PTA', 'teachers, administration and students who make up Classen is what makes it so special'), while Square reports chronic teacher absence and lack of accountability ('I have a sub at least once a day because the teachers never come to work', 'teachers dont care' and 'administration... are doing a terrible job').",
  "circle provides more rigorous, college‑preparatory coursework while square delivers inconsistent or low‑quality classroom instruction": "Circle notes a tougher workload and formal programs ('you have more homework... it will prepare you for college', 'IB... hard, grueling program'), whereas Square reports substitute-driven, video-based instruction and missing textbooks ('we have no math or spanish books', 'teachers show you YouTube videos instead of actually teaching').",

  "square exhibits more student behavior, safety, substance-use problems and punitive disciplinary practices than circle": "Square reports classroom disruptions, fights and substance use ('Students are dancing and screaming and fighting in the classrooms', 'The school does seem to have a drug problem') and punitive or inconsistent discipline ('you aren't allowed to even get your parents to send you real food during lunch without getting suspended', 'Kids were getting expelled... for being late'), whereas Circle claims an accepting, low‑bullying climate ('There's not really any bullying', 'students are tolerant, expressive and awesome').",

  "circle draws a more selectively high‑achieving, arts‑oriented peer cohort than square": "Circle repeatedly notes that the school 'takes in only the best' and that 'the cool kids are just as likely to be singers, science fair winners, dancers, or whizzes at math', implying a mission‑aligned, high‑ability peer group, while Square describes a more disengaged or problematic student population (classroom disruption, drug use, students who 'ignore you')."
}"]

["{
  "square reports more repeated high level athletic championships and state/national titles than circle": "Square lists multiple elite team titles and placements: “back to back state champions,” “cheer team are back to back national champions and Arizona State champions,” and “Pom Squad placed top 5 at Nationals,” whereas Circle only describes a “great athletic department” without repeating state or national championships.",
  "square emphasizes more extensive AP/honors course offerings and elite college acceptances than circle": "Square repeatedly cites AP/honors preparation and top-tier admissions: “lots of AP classes,” “a student from Chaparral accepted to almost every school in the country (that were applied to) including Princeton and Oberlin,” while Circle references AVID and college preparedness but gives only specific outcomes like West Point and a private college BS rather than broad elite college placement.",
  "circle reports clearer weaknesses in course variety and science instruction that square does not emphasize": "Circle explicitly states problems with offerings and science: “there is not a diverse range of classes, science department is lacking (learned little during 10th and 11th grade),” a problem not described as a central, repeated issue in Square where academics are described mainly as AP/honors-focused.",
  "circle reports lower incidence of bullying and a stronger sense of community than square, which reports cliquishness and poor newcomer integration": "Circle: “bullying is almost none existent (I have not witnessed any), strong sense of community.” Square contains repeated accounts of social exclusion and bad newcomer treatment: “a bit cliquey,” “they throw new kids to the wolves,” and parents saying new students were left on their own.",
  "square reports more extensive arts programming, frequent productions, and state/national recognition than circle": "Square details multiple arts accomplishments and productions: “We have had 4 plays this year,” “National Thespian Society,” and students “recognized throughout the state for their art,” whereas Circle notes award-winning art but complains about underfunding rather than describing broad, active arts programming.",
  "square reports more problems with administrative responsiveness and office staff behavior than circle": "Square contains several critiques of admin and staff responsiveness: “office staff is not friendly in person or on the phone,” “guidance counselor... never got back to me,” and “administration is under qualified, overwhelmed,” while Circle does not describe unresponsive administration.",
  "circle reports concrete catch-up supports and AVID-led college preparation programs more than square": "Circle names specific support structures: “many opportunities to catch up on work such as SMARTS nights, tutoring,” and “EXCELLENT avid teachers who push you to do your best,” whereas Square mentions college prep in broad terms (honors/AP) but fewer named remedial/support programs.",

  "square reports frequent safety incidents and an active threat episode with problematic staff response more than circle": "Square describes a “rumor of a gun threat” and says “the teachers punished children for leaving the school out of fear,” reporting both a serious safety incident and contested staff reaction; circle mentions disciplinary and culture issues but not gun threats or comparable acute safety events.",
  "square reports pervasive racial tension and segregation across activities more than circle": "Square explicitly states “Racism is a high ordeal” and that “races separate themselves in sports, lunches, and activities,” documenting racial segregation in daily school life; circle includes no mention of racial tension or segregation.",
  "square reports an over‑reliance on suspension and blanket punishment policies more than circle": "Square says leadership “use a blanket solution... suspension” and “They discipline more than teach,” criticizing punitive discipline as routine and ineffective; circle criticizes unfair rule application but does not describe suspension as the school’s primary disciplinary tactic.",
  "square reports overloaded counseling/guidance resources and poor absentee notification practices more than circle": "Square reports the “guidance office and social worker are overloaded with problem students” and a parent asks “why don't you contact me, or other parents when their kids are absent?,” indicating strained student support services and weak attendance communication; circle contains no comparable statements about counseling load or absence notification.",

["{

  "square reports pervasive bullying and ineffective administrative response more than circle": "Square repeatedly documents bullying and failure of staff to stop it: “if your not in with the jocks and preps your going to be bullied,” and “The superintedant won't do anything for your problems, neither will the prinicpal,” while Circle includes complaints about student behavior but does not repeatedly attribute widespread unresolved bullying to administrative inaction.",
  "circle reports stricter discipline with frequent suspensions and detentions more than square": "Circle criticizes punitive enforcement: “These children are always either suspended or in detention… the rules are TOO strict,” and a parent threatens to transfer a child because of discipline, whereas Square portrays discipline as lax or inconsistently applied rather than uniformly strict.",
  "square reports poor instructional quality, lack of extra help, and teacher favoritism more than circle": "Square contains concrete complaints about teaching and support: “The only thing I learned was basic algebra… There is no extra help from this teachers, and barely any teaching going on,” and “The only way you can pass… is if your one of the teachers pets,” while Circle repeatedly cites caring, knowledgeable, and dedicated teachers and offers examples of student supports.",
  "square reports specific facility and health/sanitation failures more than circle": "Square lists concrete facility/health issues: “bedbug issue they never informed the parents” and “take care of the smoking in the bathrooms,” whereas Circle’s comments focus on programming, staff, and safety patrols and do not mention bedbugs or facility sanitation failures.",

["{
  "circle emphasizes a faith based/Catholic identity more than square": "Circle explicitly identifies itself as a Catholic school multiple times (e.g., “William V Fisher catholic High School,” “Fisher Catholic,” “FCHS”), while Square’s reviews make no mention of any religious or faith-based identity or programming.",
  "circle reports explicit, approachable administrative leadership and clear mission more than square": "Circle states “The school's leadership is outstanding and operates with a clear vision and mission” and “The prinipal is extremely approachable,” whereas Square only notes that “the teachers care as well as the administration” without describing vision, leadership quality, or accessibility.",
  "circle provides concrete, testable academic program evidence (OGTs, AP course list, AP test plans) more than square": "Circle names specific measurable academic elements: “Students at Fisher score very well on the OGTs,” lists four AP classes “(AP English, Chem, Calc, Euro),” and notes a plan to take five AP tests; Square gives no standardized test or course-list details.",
  "circle reports limited AP course offerings (only four AP classes) whereas square does not report such course limitations": "Circle explicitly notes a constraint: “the school only offers four AP classes (AP English, Chem, Calc, Euro),” while Square makes no mention of AP availability or limits.",
  "circle emphasizes small school size as a concrete feature contributing to community more than square": "Circle repeatedly links smallness to community—“The school is small enough that every one knows one another,” “everyone knows everyone”—whereas Square praises family feeling but does not describe school size as a structural factor.",
  "circle describes strong competitive academic teams and interscholastic competition (Quiz Bowl, national competitions) more than square": "Circle reports that despite size it “consistently has one of the best quiz teams in the state and regularly qualifies and competes in national academic competitions,” while Square mentions band participation but no competitive academic teams.",
  "circle emphasizes development of critical thinking and readiness for adulthood more than square": "Circle claims students “are taught to think critically” and a student reports the school “has helped form me into a responsible young adult ready to venture into the real world,” whereas Square focuses on graduation and university attendance without explicit statements about critical thinking or life-readiness curricula.",
  "circle highlights school spirit and community service involvement more than square": "Circle explicitly says “we have tons of school spirit and love to help the community!” while Square mentions togetherness and family but does not reference school spirit events or community service activities.",
  "square reports at least one problematic teacher where circle reports none": "Square specifically notes “they were only 1 bad teacher I thought was honestly a bad teacher that was an English teacher,” while Circle’s comments about faculty are uniformly positive (e.g., “The faculty is excellent and demonstrate commitment to student success”).",
  "square highlights music program participation (band) more than circle": "Square specifically names student participation in Band—“i love participating in the Band”—while Circle’s extracurricular mentions focus on quiz bowl, sports and clubs, not music participation.",
  "square emphasizes alumni college progression and on-time graduation as primary outcome evidence more than circle": "Square uses outcome anecdotes—“My children both graduate from this high school and went on to major universities and graduated on time”—whereas Circle emphasizes standardized test scores, AP coursework, and competitive academic achievements as outcome evidence."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports declining enrollment and budget pressure more than square": "Circle reviewers state financial strain explicitly: “Enrollment is down below the operating budget,” and warn the school “might not be there in ten years,” whereas Square reviews include no mention of enrollment shortfalls or operating-budget concerns.",
  "square reports more frequent violent incidents, gang activity, and drug presence than circle": "Square contains direct safety claims: “Gang activity, constant fights, and a huge presence of drugs within the school,” and descriptions of frequent fights; Circle reviews describe bullying and social exclusion but do not report gangs, widespread fights, or drugs.",
  "circle emphasizes small size and sustained one on one teacher relationships more than square": "Circle repeatedly highlights smallness and personalized attention: “It's a small school (60 kids per grade) … one on one attention … The teachers are amazing, and the relationships you build with them are eternal,” while Square emphasizes larger, mixed-sized classes and less of a sustained small-school intimacy.",
  "square documents arbitrary and inconsistent administrative discipline practices more than circle": "Square reports administrative arbitrariness with concrete examples: the assistant principal “draws names out of a hat each day… Those are the students who must follow dress code,” and a biased coach creates exceptions; Circle criticizes leadership changes and favoritism but lacks the same examples of random rule-enforcement.",
  "circle reports limited high school course offerings and teacher absenteeism more than square": "Circle reviewers state that “the high school curriculum struggles to offer all classes required” and that “teachers are never even in the classroom… If they do show up, they usually give you the assignment,” while Square lists concrete program offerings (AP, arts, NJROTC) and course variety.",
  "square reports overcrowded and uneven class sizes more than circle": "Square gives explicit classroom-size problems: “one class with over 30 kids and in the next have 18-20,” and students shuffled between classes; Circle describes small cohorts (60 per grade) and no similar overcrowding complaints.",
  "circle reports rising tuition and affordability concerns more than square": "Circle mentions cost pressure: “The price is going up but the education is going down,” and parents making “sacrifices to keep them in private school,” whereas Square (a public high school) includes no tuition or affordability issues.",
  "circle displays stronger social insularity and exclusion of outsiders than square": "Circle reviewers warn outsiders struggle to fit in: “If you are not a family resident of the area of Somerville, you will have trouble fitting in,” and note punishment of students who are “different,” whereas Square contains multiple mentions of a diverse student body and at least one reviewer saying “Being of a different race isn't seen as a problem.”",
  "square reports stronger, named arts and NJROTC programs more than circle": "Square reviewers list specific, active programs: “math and arts (Graphic, Web, Photography, Intro, and Theatre)” and “The NJROTC program… helps guide the students,” while Circle reviews do not describe comparable arts or ROTC program presence.",
  "circle reports higher standardized test and scholarship outcomes more than square": "Circle contains claims of strong metrics and college awards: “The percentage of students scoring 30 and above on the ACT… incredible” and students receiving scholarships, whereas Square reviewers claim “Most of the kids in the isd are not prepared for college” and describe fewer high-achieving peers.",
  "square reports concrete on-campus safety/property incidents more than circle": "Square documents actionable safety/property failures: “Some of the men's bathrooms are closed due to theft” and “someone set a soap dispenser on fire” causing a pulled alarm; Circle reviews recount behavioral and cultural problems but do not report these types of facility-targeted incidents.",
  "circle reports technological stagnation and resistance to adopting modern technology more than square": "Circle remarks explicitly on tech lag and leadership resistance: “My computer teacher wanted to switch to Mac but the headmaster said no… There's no forward thinking here,” while Square mentions aging physical fixtures (e.g., “20 year old lockers”) but not a similar narrative of blocked technology upgrades.",
  "square reports a higher prevalence of long tenured, experienced teachers than circle": "Square reviewers note teacher longevity and subject expertise: “Many of my teachers had been on the MCHS staff for years, and their expertise and experience were evident,” while Circle reviews include multiple complaints about inconsistent teacher presence and variable teaching quality."
}"]

  "square emphasizes strong extracurricular music and athletics offerings and outcomes more than circle": "Square gives many concrete extracurricular examples and outcomes (\"marching band, pep band, jazz ensemble, orchestra\", \"played in the pit for the musicals\", \"coaches TOP NOTCH\", \"athletic programs routinely go to regional and state competitions\"), while Circle mentions no extracurricular programs or student achievements.",
  "square documents special education service failures and IEP/IDEA noncompliance whereas circle does not": "Square reports explicit special-education problems and procedural noncompliance (\"serious deficiencies with special education and students with IEP's\", \"disregard for the IDEA laws and refusals to offer specialized assistance\"), a topic absent from Circle.",
  "circle reports pervasive lack of disciplinary enforcement on bullying more than square": "Circle states the school \"does nothing to stop this\" and that when offenders are \"caught is a slap on the hand but they keep bulling\", presenting school-wide discipline failure as the central issue; Square mentions bullying but mixes praise and criticism rather than presenting blanket inaction.",
  "circle cites specific classroom policy violations (hoods allowed) and teachers not following through that square does not": "Circle gives an operational policy example: \"students are allowed to use their hoods during class some teachers don t follow through with discipline,\" whereas Square contains no report of this specific classroom-rule violation.",
  "square reports active parental/community engagement and alumni/long-term student outcomes more than circle": "Square references parent involvement and long-term outcomes (\"active parent involvement\", \"my son... is now a music major at U of L\", \"my daughter has moved back to the Floyd Central area so that her children can come back to good schools\"), whereas Circle contains no community or alumni outcome examples.",
  "square provides quantifiable recognitions and course counts while circle provides none": "Square lists numeric achievements and offerings (\"fifteen Indiana Four Star Recognitions\", \"two national Blue Ribbon School\", \"23 dual credit courses and 18 AP courses\"), but Circle offers no comparable quantitative data about school performance or offerings.",
  "square treats multiple concrete school functions (academics, extracurriculars, special education, administration) while circle focuses almost exclusively on bullying/discipline": "Square discusses a range of in-building practices and outcomes (academic programs, music and sports success, special education failures, parent involvement, awards), whereas Circle is narrowly centered on bullying and enforcement of rules.",
  "square references formal compliance and meeting processes (CCC meetings, IDEA) whereas circle does not": "Square mentions procedural/oversight elements tied to special education (\"Just sitting through a CCC meeting you can see the disregard for the IDEA laws\"), invoking formal compliance processes absent from Circle."
}"]

["{
  "square highlights high-profile competitive marching band success whereas circle does not": "Square explicitly cites marching band competitive prestige: “They won first place for 4A at the Texas UIL State Championships in 2011” and repeatedly praises the band as a program and family; Circle contains no mention of a competitive marching band or comparable high‑profile arts competition success.",
  "square reports excessive possibly rule‑violating extracurricular practice time causing student burnout while circle does not": "Square states the school “openly appears to violate UIL limitations on summer and after-school practice time for marching band and other competitive programs” and that this “wins UIL tournaments, but burns out the kids,” whereas Circle does not describe excessive or rule‑breaking extracurricular time.",
  "square raises district-level massive debt and property tax consequences whereas circle does not": "Square includes district fiscal detail and community impact: “as a District we are $3.7 BILLION dollars in debt…property taxes (which average $6,000 per year) are causing the resale value of our homes to go down,” a district‑level complaint absent from Circle.",
  "circle documents successful dual enrollment and advanced coursework completion whereas square mentions AP offerings but not dual enrollment": "Circle reports concrete college credit outcomes: “my daughter graduated with four college classes completed through Dual Enrollment,” while Square discusses AP courses and AP focus (“Except for AP classes…”) but provides no dual enrollment completion evidence.",
  "circle reports explicit responsive support from administrators for students and families whereas square reports administrative neglect and lack of follow-up": "Circle gives a named example of administrative support: “the staff from the principal, Mr. Hood, all staff has been very understanding and works well with me and my granddaughter” and “The teachers and administrators care about the students,” whereas Square includes multiple claims of neglect: “teachers, counselors, AP are not helpful…no one in admin cares to contact parent” when students stop attending.",
  "square reports incidents of bullying and racial harassment while circle does not": "Square contains explicit accounts of bullying including a racial harassment claim: “I am a black male in the 10th grade and I cannot stand this school there are many people that bully me and pick on me because of my race,” whereas Circle contains no reports of bullying or racial targeting.",
  "square alleges widespread teacher incompetence and failures of instructional leadership whereas circle mainly reports teacher care and school improvement": "Square repeatedly asserts poor instruction and leadership problems: “More than half of the teachers at CPHS needed to be fired…they either don't know their material or don't care” and “No instructional leadership,” while Circle mostly praises staff care and improvement—“The teachers and administrators care about the students” and “The school has improved dramatically over the last two years.”",
  "square notes limited foreign language offerings and lagging world language programs whereas circle does not": "Square criticizes language programming: “it and the rest of LISD fall way behind in foreign language learning…feeder middle schools generally offer only Spanish I to 8th graders,” while Circle includes no commentary on world language availability.",
  "square emphasizes prioritization of winning extracurricular programs over student welfare and academics whereas circle emphasizes academic progress and support": "Square contains statements that athletics and band are prioritized at the expense of other concerns: “They care about winning in football and marching band nothing else matters,” and notes burnout and neglect; Circle emphasizes academic outcomes and support, e.g. students in advanced classes with A’s and administrative support aiding a student through family issues.",
  "circle includes at least one report of failing to meet state standards while square contains no mention of state accountability results": "Circle opens with a review asserting the school “didn't even meet state standards last year,” whereas Square has no reviewer comment about state accountability ratings or failing to meet state standards."
}"]

  "square enforces inflexible credit and graduation policies that blocked an otherwise qualified student from graduating on time, circle does not report this": "Square describes a concrete administrative policy outcome: because HAHS “does not” offer drivers education the reviewer’s daughter was “2 credits shy of graduating on time,” and the principal “gave no option other than for her to complete another year of school,” forcing the student to quit four weeks before graduation.",
  "square lacks practical, credit-bearing programs like drivers education that caused graduation barriers, circle does not mention such missing programs": "Square explicitly notes that the previous school “offered drivers education, HAHS does not,” and links that absence to a credit shortfall; Circle’s review makes no mention of missing practical or vocational credit-bearing programs.",
  "square reports administrator insults and disrespectful staff behavior (including a derogatory accent comment) whereas circle does not report comparable staff-level abuse": "Square quotes the principal saying, “You'd better loose than southern accent and learn to talk like a coal cracker,” and frames that as memorable and harmful; Circle does not describe similar insulting behavior by administrators or staff.",
  "square reports increased security measures and deliberate teacher turnover perceived as lowering teacher qualifications, circle does not mention these changes": "Square claims “they now have metal detectors at HAHS” and that the district “paid many of the teachers … to take early retirement in order to get new, and probably less-qualified, teachers in there,” while Circle contains no report of metal detectors or district-driven staff buyouts.",
  "circle reports poor athletic program outcomes (especially football) that square does not describe": "Circle singles out athletics as a problem, saying the “football team is a disaster. Can't even win a game,” a concrete program outcome absent from Square’s account.",
  "circle describes a problematic student social composition that interferes with learning, square does not": "Circle characterizes the student body as “inbred annoying brats who interfere with the integrity of the learning effort,” attributing learning disruption to peer culture; Square does not make a comparable claim about the student population’s social composition.",
  "square reports graduates with gaps in basic civic knowledge and poor overall college/life readiness while circle reports students being prepared for college": "Square asserts, “Kids are actually graduating from this school and have no idea who JFK or MLK are” and that students are “not prepared for life, college,” whereas Circle claims its courses are “preparing for college” and the reviewer recommends the school for teens seeking college preparation."
}"]

  "circle reports a Bible-based Christian curriculum and faith integration while square does not": "Circle explicitly states “It is a bible based curriculum” and repeatedly references Christian faith and churches represented (“Students seem passionate about & value Christian faith… about 100 different churchs are represented”), while square contains no mention of religion or faith-based programming.",
  "circle lists concrete program offerings (VPK, AP, arts, sports) and program strengths/limitations while square lists none": "Circle names and evaluates multiple programs—VPK, AP courses, arts (plays, choral, band, dance, art), and many sports—e.g. “My son went to VPK…,” “Minimal AP courses available,” “The school plays are pretty good… choral and band has improved… Sports: This is what the school is primarily known for.” Square contains no program inventory or specific program assessments.",
  "circle documents reported bullying, cliques, and racism inside the school whereas square does not raise safety/social-culture incidents": "Multiple circle reviews describe bullying and cliques (“there was bullying going on and lots of cliques,” “I've seen more hateful behavior and cliques…”) and an explicit claim of racial problems (“Racism is rampant”), while square makes no claims about bullying, cliques, or racial climate.",
  "circle reports administrative instability and frequent leadership changes while square does not": "Circle contains statements about turnover undermining the school: “over the pst 5 years there have been 4-5 administrative changes which has really undone much of the work Providence has succeeded at,” whereas square does not mention leadership change or administrative stability.",
  "circle reports academic integrity problems and grade inflation/cheating and athlete favoritism while square does not": "Circle includes accusations such as “Almost every students cheats on assignments,” “Everyone gets straight A’s all you have to do is email a teacher,” and “athletes get away with lower standards,” while square only questions score reporting and does not mention classroom cheating, grade inflation, or preferential treatment for athletes.",
  "circle reports strong family involvement and small-to-medium class sizes while square provides no enrollment or family engagement detail": "Circle asserts “Tons of family involvement” and “small to medium size classes” alongside “It's also big in size for those who like a larger population,” giving a picture of parental engagement and class-size, whereas square offers no information about family involvement or class sizes.",
  "circle gives mixed but specific performance claims (high SAT ranking, AP limitations) while square focuses narrowly on suspected manipulation of math percentages": "Circle claims concrete historical performance (“Providence students had the 4th highest SAT scores in Duval County… top 10 in the entire State”) but also notes limitations (“Minimal AP courses available”), whereas square’s sole substantive claim is skepticism about reported math percentages (“I would question of these percentages of math scores because I know that those results have a chance of being fixed”).",
  "circle mentions affordability and tuition barriers affecting enrollment while square does not": "Circle contains a parent stating cost is a barrier: “Unfortunately, I can't financially afford for my son to continue his education there,” indicating tuition/affordability constraints, while square includes no information about cost or accessibility.",
  "circle highlights staff behaviors and moral modeling (teachers, coaches, counselors) while square does not describe staff conduct beyond generational decline": "Circle includes multiple observations about staff—positive: “The teachers at this school are top notch,” “Every single person working there is enthusiastic…,” and moral modeling: “They model a life of honesty and integrity”; square does not provide any descriptions of teacher, coach, or counselor behaviors beyond a general comment that the school has declined.",
  "square reports a long-term perceived institutional decline over decades that circle does not characterize in the same way": "Square states a multidecade deterioration: “Hattiesburg High School has really gone downhill since I graduated from there back in 1987,” framing change as long-term decline since the 1980s; circle contains complaints and praise but does not frame the school as having uniformly declined over several decades.",
  "circle reports distinct extracurricular strengths and weaknesses (athletics strong, arts improving) while square gives no extracurricular assessment": "Circle explicitly says athletics are a primary strength and details recruitment and coaching (“Sports: This is what the school is primarily known for… very capable coaches and teams”), and separately rates arts as improving (“The arts department has certainly risen from the dead… school plays are pretty good”), whereas square offers no assessment of extracurricular activities."
}"]

    "circle reports elimination of electives and extracurricular cuts leading to fewer creative outlets than square": "Circle complains \"all the elective courses that have been axed out of the curriculum....there is no creative outlet for the students\" and that \"The intra and extracurricular cuts sadden me,\" whereas Square describes elective classes as low quality but does not report schoolwide elimination of electives or broad extracurricular cuts.",
    "square highlights a strong music program led by a specific committed teacher whereas circle does not mention any strong specialized program": "Square explicitly praises the band as \"phenomenal\" and credits the band teacher Mrs. Kade for teaching responsibility and criticism, noting the program makes student growth possible; Circle does not point to any comparable thriving program or named staff member leading an extracurricular.",
    "square describes a clear honors and AP pathway that prepares students for college with AP exam success more than circle": "Square repeatedly advises taking \"honor/ap classes\" and reports \"I ended up passing all the AP exams I took\" and that AP/honors students have gone on to success in college and graduate programs; Circle gives a single alumni claim of degree attainment but lacks organized evidence of a current honors/AP pathway or AP exam outcomes.",
    "circle reports pandemic-era leadership failures and hypocrisy around safety policies while square omits pandemic issues": "Circle accuses a leader named Steven Dickerson of poor pandemic decisions, noting \"They allow sports with strangers during pandemic but do not allow kids to attend school full time\" and that he was \"seen out playing in a golf outing with 70 people without a mask,\" while Square contains no references to pandemic policy or leadership behavior.",
    "circle cites limited resources and lack of space hindering student support more than square": "Circle states teachers \"can only go so far with so limited resources\" and that \"Kids who need extra help are not being helped he sights lack of space,\" indicating resource and space constraints affecting support; Square criticizes course quality but does not cite systemic resource or space shortages.",
    "square reports stark class track quality differences with regular classes labeled a joke and favoritism in electives whereas circle praises teachers broadly": "Square asserts \"The regular classes are a joke\" and that \"teachers in those classes played favorites,\" distinguishing weak regular-track instruction from stronger honors/AP classes, whereas Circle says \"most of the teachers are capable and are doing their best to instruct the students\" without describing such intra-school instructional disparity.",
    "square emphasizes student self-motivation and independent studying as central to preparedness more than circle": "Square repeatedly stresses that success depends on students' initiative—\"The secret to success ... is finding motivation in yourself to study on your own\" and warns \"If you slack in high school, then you play catch up in college\"—while Circle focuses on institutional failures (bullying, cuts, leadership) rather than promoting student-driven study habits.",
    "circle describes administrative focus on building projects and ceremonial events over instructional needs more than square": "Circle criticizes leadership for prioritizing a \"ceremonial ground breaking for the new school\" while students have only \"spent 5 days in class during the first month\" and lacking full-time instruction, indicating perceived administrative emphasis on facilities/events over immediate education; Square contains no similar claim about administrative priorities favoring facilities or ceremonies."
}"]

  "square reports lax enforcement of smoking and drug-related policies in bathrooms more than circle": "Square reports policy enforcement failures onsite: “smokers in the bathroom!... they allow certain kids to smoke in the nurses bathroom” and later notes students bringing drugs: “students who bring large amoints of drgs on campus.” Circle includes no similar reports of on-campus smoking/drug policy failures.",

  "square reports a strong arts program more than circle": "Square offers a positive program-specific claim: “The arts program is amazing, their teachers care,” while circle's program-specific mentions focus on athletics and general support networks rather than arts offerings.",
  "square alleges administrative manipulation of electives and donation votes more than circle": "Square accuses administrative procedural misconduct: “This school will alter votes on donations and says that you choose the electives, even though they will force electives on you.” Circle contains no comparable claim about altering votes or forced elective assignment.",
  "circle contains calls for radical restructuring or school closure by reviewers more than square": "Circle includes extreme parent calls about remedies: “This school is a joke and should be shut down or totally re-staffed,” indicating reviewers request wholesale institutional change; square voices transfers and recommendations to attend other schools but not explicit calls to close or fully re-staff the school.",
  "square reports intrusive security presence and student misconduct concerns more than circle": "Square states security is 'always up everyone's business' and links that to drug concerns: “security always up everyone's business, and students who bring large amoints of drgs on campus.” Circle does not describe intrusive security practices or on-campus security enforcement as a salient issue.",
  "circle reports culturally or linguistically fraught interactions with leadership more than square": "Circle notes a specific cultural/language tension affecting parent trust: “The Principal who has been there for 10 years, does not speak English correctly...   "circle reports use of varied instructional materials to create personal connections more than square": "Circle says \"Educators at Yorktown have a variety of materials to show personal connections that create a connection from the knowledge to the student,\" a concrete practice (use of diverse materials to link content to students) that Square does not mention.",
  "circle emphasizes fostering student autonomy and reinforcement for good behavior more than square": "Circle notes students \"learn autonomy\" and \"needs reinforcement for good behavior,\" indicating instructional/behavioral practices aimed at autonomy and positive reinforcement; Square instead describes disciplinary policing by administration (see below) rather than fostering autonomy.",
  "square exhibits administrative dysfunction and punitive discipline focus more than circle": "Square contains concrete accusations about leadership: \"administration shows more interest in expelling children than educating them\" and \"The administrators for West Ottawa High School lack the ability to communicate effectively with the families,\" showing a punitive and poorly communicative administration that Circle does not report.",
  "square reports insufficient staffing and limited course availability causing waiting lists more than circle": "Square claims \"What lacks is having enough teachers to provide the classes that children want to take\" and complains about \"waiting list for students to take Honors classes or Foreign languages,\" a concrete staffing and course-availability problem not described in Circle.",
  "square reports resource allocation choices and facility cleanliness problems more than circle": "Square accuses the school of budget priorities that favor \"coffee bars and TV's\" while having \"no money for custodians to keep the buildings clean,\" a specific facilities/funding complaint absent from Circle.",
  "square reports visible security presence in halls more than circle": "Square specifically notes safety staffing: \"It's safe to be in the hall's because there are a lot of security guards around,\" describing an explicit security practice that Circle does not mention.",
  "square reports teachers are praised but undermined by administration and resource limits more than circle": "Square includes praise for teachers and programs but says these are negated by leadership and resourcing: \"If not for the administration... ["{
  "circle enforces selective admissions and mandatory college-application requirements more than square": "Circle reviews state explicit entry/exit requirements: “We were required to maintain a 2.5 GPA to attend Sumner” and “You have to apply and be accepted to 3 colleges before you can graduate,” whereas Square contains no mention of selective admission or formal college-application graduation requirements.",
  "circle shows stronger college preparatory curriculum and reported college readiness outcomes than square": "Circle describes explicit college-preparatory focus and outcomes: “It is a college PREPARATORY school” and “I received a phenomenal education at Sumner Academy. I was far better prepared for college,” while Square repeatedly cites lower academic levels and disengagement: “The level at which students are asked to perform is lower than at most schools” and many reports of disengaged students.",
  "circle provides more sustained arts and music programming and visible student art displays than square": "Circle highlights multiple thriving arts offerings and displays: “The music program was very nice… The art department was excellent, and you can see the years of students' art decorating the hallways and library.” Square has occasional positive mentions of band but no comparable sustained arts display or program emphasis.",
  "circle reports more consistent teacher competence and student support services than square": "Circle statements emphasize teacher quality and support: “The teachers were very competent… there was plenty of support for those of us who needed a little more help,” while Square repeatedly reports poor teacher performance and lack of care: “only two that are great teachers, the rest are lazy… Most of the instructors do not care.”",
  "circle has stricter fight-discipline policies and far fewer fights than square": "Circle claims very low fight incidence tied to strict enforcement: “There are almost no fights (last year had first fight in 10 years!!!) because you get in a fight and you are expelled no exceptions.” Square reports ongoing fights and poor supervision: “I have also witnessed… fighting during this time,” indicating less effective enforcement and higher incidence.",
  "circle suffers more severe facility hygiene and pest problems than square": "Circle repeatedly reports pest and sanitation issues: “there are so many roaches throughout the entire building… awful sewage smell on the third floor and the ladies rooms are filthy,” while Square's reviews mention facility/design problems but do not report pervasive roach infestation or sewage odors.",
  "square exhibits administrative disorganization and lost enrollment paperwork more than circle": "Square reports concrete administrative failures: “They lost the school they were transferring in from paperwork, and they put my kids in classes they had already completed,” and reviewers call administration “disorganized, detached,” whereas Circle describes responsive staff and organized academic supports.",
  "square applies more rigid, punitive attendance/documentation rules than circle": "Square reviews describe strict absence documentation and punitive follow-up: “even if your kids are excussed from school with a doctors note, the school will send you court papers… you must have a doctors note or other agency note…and no more than 10 notes via parents in a year,” while Circle does not report comparable attendance-documentation enforcement.",
  "square reports grade irregularities or disappearing grades affecting athletic eligibility more than circle": "Square contains a concrete allegation of grade manipulation: “Missing grades on the parent portal 'disappeared.'… his overall grade was a mid-level D,” which reviewers tie to athletic eligibility; Circle includes no examples of missing/altered grades.",
  "square shows more on-campus drug activity and unsafe behavior in student parking areas than circle": "Square reviews provide eyewitness reports of criminal and reckless behavior in parking: “I have also witnessed drugs being bought and sold… students riding around on the top of vehicles… because there is absolutely no supervision in the student parking lot,” while Circle explicitly notes strong safety/climate and almost no fights, with no drug reports.",
  "square engages in shaming or denial of lunch to students more than circle": "Square recounts active mistreatment at lunch lines: “give any student that may have forgotten their lunch or lunch money a really hard time about eating in a public school laughing in their face,” whereas Circle’s lunch problem is contamination by pests (“roaches are often times found in their food”), not deliberate shaming or denial by staff.",
  "square suffers more problematic building design and traffic/parking hazards than circle": "Square reviewers call the facility design unsafe and logistically harmful: “The design is seriously flawed and possibly even a fire hazard… coming and going from this place is an absolute nightmare… being late to work every day,” while Circle mentions aging facilities and restroom issues but not dangerous design or parking-gridlock causing consistent lateness.",
  "circle offers fewer course choices but highlights teachers compensating for that limitation more than square": "Circle admits limited course variety: “The classes offered were a little minimalistic, but was made up for by very competent teachers,” whereas Square’s complaints center on low rigor and engagement across classes rather than limited course selection.",
  "square elicits stronger community outrage and calls for school closure than circle": "Square contains extreme community reactions and threats of external escalation: “This school should be closed!!! … I am going to Fox news and I will make sure that the entire nation knows,” while Circle reviews, despite criticisms about facilities, include multiple endorsements like “Would send my own children here in a heartbeat” and no calls for closure."
}"]

["{
  "circle reports ineffective school counseling that prevented some students from graduating whereas square does not": "Circle states explicitly: \"Our school counselors did not give us counseling in fact some students could not graduate their senior years due to poor counseling.\" Square contains no comparable claim about counselors preventing graduation.",
  "circle reports a large disciplinarian staff and strict dress codes whereas square does not mention those policies": "Circle says the school \"was more concerned with keeping us in line by having a large disciplinarian staff and strict dress codes.\" Square discusses student fights and staff but includes no description of a heavy discipline apparatus or dress-code enforcement.",
  "circle reports heavy use of Teach for America / inexperienced teachers while square does not emphasize that staffing source": "Circle: \"We were already filled with Teach for America Teachers by this time and most of them were not prepared for the type of attitudes the children have.\" Square criticizes some teachers but does not identify a TFA presence or blame a specific short-term staffing program.",
  "square reports explicit teacher communication practices (email responsiveness) that circle does not": "Square says \"They all gave out their email addresses and were quick to answer any questions we had,\" indicating an organized, responsive teacher communication practice that circle does not describe.",
  "circle reports absence of tutoring and art programs whereas square describes available after-school clubs and activities": "Circle states bluntly: \"There were no tutoring programs and no art programs either.\" By contrast, square lists \"plenty of clubs and organizations for after-school activities as well,\" showing available extracurricular offerings.",
  "square documents specific physical resource decay (falling apart textbooks and lockers) more than circle": "Square gives concrete examples: \"most of the textbooks and lockers are falling apart\" and \"the books they give us are either falling apart or close too.\" Circle only states the school \"was underfunded\" without the same level of physical-resource detail.",
  "circle reports a school assembly encouraging students to drop out for factory work whereas square does not": "Circle describes a disturbing incident: \"we had an assembly... persuading us to drop out and work for the Domino Sugar plant... if we dropped out that day we could make 30k a year.\" Square contains no comparable claim about school-sponsored dropout encouragement.",
  "circle reports graduates unprepared for university and struggling to form study habits whereas square emphasizes that students can succeed if motivated": "Circle: \"I was not prepared for university and struggled to form studying habits.\" Square repeatedly says \"you could learn and do well there if you wanted to,\" indicating the school presents opportunity conditional on student motivation.",
  "circle asserts the school is \"very safe\" while square reports frequent fights and bullying incidents": "Circle opens with \"My school is a very safe school.\" In contrast, square says \"Alot of fights happen at MHS\" and reports bullying/name-calling: \"they talked smack behind my back and sometimes called me names.\"",
  "square calls for more parent involvement and names leadership decisions as problematic whereas circle does not raise parent involvement": "Square explicitly requests \"MORE PARENT INVOLVEMENT!\" and states \"I did not personally have very good experiences with the school leadership. I was very disappointed in several of their decisions.\" Circle makes no comparable appeal about parents or critique of leadership-level decisions.",
  "square highlights student body diversity as a celebrated strength whereas circle does not mention diversity": "Square says \"What I love most about MHS is the diversity... that is actually celebrated at this high school.\" Circle contains no mention of student diversity or celebration of backgrounds.",
  "square reports poor food quality and a football funding bias that circle does not describe": "Square complains \"The food is horrible\" and that \"the only thing MHS cares about is Football... while the other sports are forgotten about,\" concrete claims about food and funding priorities not present in circle."
}"]

  "circle reports active campus supervision via hall monitors whereas square does not describe comparable supervision practices": "Circle notes a specific supervision practice: \"there are many hall monitors there to help supervisor the campus,\" framed as giving parents \"peace of mind.\" Square does not describe hall monitors or similar campus supervisory staffing in any review."
